REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN SASKATCHEWAN LEGISLATURE
speechtext:
Before the business of the house is proceeded with may I say that in the Ottawa Citizen of Saturday, March 4, there appears on page 9 a report of a meeting of the Saskatchewan legislature. In the course of that report Mr. Carl Stewart, member for Yorkton, Saskatchewan, is reported to have said:
I make the charge that Mr. Coldwell, Mr. Castleden and Mr. Feeley have improperly interfered with the board to keep men out of uniform.
Mr. Feeley is a member of the Saskatchewan legislature, and the board referred to is the moboiization board. I wish to say that the charge is wholly false, and comes from a person of whom the present chairman of the mobilization board, Mr. Justice Anderson, said on December 4, 1943, that "people who know Mr. Stewart would not take his criticism too seriously."

speechtext:
On February 28 I told the house that the list of the members of the Canadian army who have received decorations for gallantry in this war would be tabled just as soon as a number of recent operational awards had been gazetted. Those latest awards have now been gazetted and appear in the special edition of the Canada Gazette published today.
I now have the privilege of submitting to the house the names of almost five hundred members of the Canadian army to whom honours have been awarded by His Majesty for deeds of gallantry and devotion to duty in this war. With the unanimous permission of the house I would ask that these names be given a permanent record on Hansard.
_ With the exception of the Victoria Cross, it is not the practice to publish the citations showing the detailed circumstances under which

the awards were earned. In the case of the award of the Victoria Cross the practice is to publish not only the name but the citation as well. That decoration, as the house knows, is the highest award for valour and devotion to duty that can be conferred on a member of the fighting forces by his king.
There are two awards of the Victoria Cross in the list which I am submitting to-day. One has already been published. It is the award to Lieutenant-Colonel Cecil Merritt for heroic and inspiring leadership at Dieppe. The citation appeared in the Canada Gazette of October 10, 1942. I shall read it, Mr. Speaker, in order that it may be on Hansard'.
The King has been graciously pleased to approve the award of the Victoria Cross to:
Lieutenant-Colonel Charles Cecil Ingersoll Merritt, the South Saskatchewan Regiment.
For matchless gallantry and inspiring leadership whilst commanding his battalion during the Dieppe raid on the 19th August, 1942.
From the point of landing, his unit's advance had to be made across a bridge in Pourville which was swept by very heavy machine-gun, mortar and artillery fire; the first parties were mostly destroyed and the bridge thickly covered by their bodies. A daring lead was required; waving his helmet, Lieutenant-Colonel Merritt rushed forward shouting "Come on over! There's nothing to worry about here."
He thus personally led the survivors of at least four parties in turn across the bridge. Quickly organizing these, he led them forward and when held up by enemy pill-boxes he again headed rushes which succeeded in clearing them. In one case he himself destroyed the occupants of the post by throwing grenades into it. After several of his runners became casualties, he himself kept contact with his different positions.
Although twice wounded Lieutenant-Colonel Merritt continued to direct the unit's operations with great vigour and determination and while organizing the withdrawal he stalked a sniper with a Bren gun and silenced him. He then coolly gave orders for the departure and announced his intention to hold off and "get even with" the enemy. When last seen he was collecting Bren and tommy guns and preparing a defensive position which successfully covered the withdrawal from the beach.
Lieutenant-Colonel Merritt is now reported to be a prisoner of war.
To this commanding officer's personal daring the success of his unit's operations and the safe reembarkation of a large portion of it were chiefly due.
If the minister would allow me to do so I should like to add that this man is also a great grandson of a former prime minister of this country, Sir Charles Tupper, one of the greatest of Canadians.

I rose particularly to make a personal reference in connection with this matter, for which I hope I may be pardoned. Before war broke out a young man, William Manley, went from my own town of Brampton and became a private in the British army. In the early battles in Libya, in 1941, he died at his post after displaying such gallantry that he was posthumously awarded the Victoria Cross. We are very proud of this young man, and I thought that pride should be shared by this parliament and this nation.

I wish to table return No. 435, moved for by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair), in respect to soldier settlers who signed quit claim deeds or who were served with repossession notices, and so on, asking the dates of the original purchase in each case, and similar questions. For the information of my hon. friend, and by way of apology and perhaps explanation, I want to say that this motion first appeared on the order paper last June in the form of a question. On July 1, 1943, it was passed as an order for return, so that considerable time has elapsed since the order was passed. I may say, by way of apology to my hon. friend for the delay, that the return did involve a considerable amount of work. I asked the treasury official in the department to give me a summary of the time spent in preparing the reply, and the value of the time so required. I find that two senior members of the accounting staff, Mr. Woolsey and Mr. Little, were employed for two months, on an average salary of $230 per month. Then, four of the clerical staff were employed for two months in assembling detail, and their average salary was $125 a month. In addition, three typists were employed for a week in typing and checking the final return, and for that time their salaries aggregated $60. In addition to these I find that one senior clerk was employed for one month reviewing files and records of acreage development over an average of twenty-three years, and also looking up values at dates of rescission. This service cost $200. I give 
this information to my hon. friend in explanation of the delay. The full value of time employed in preparing the answer to the return was $2,180.

I thank the minister for bringing down this information. I had a specific reason for getting it. I believe if the minister would compare some of the hardships endured by those settlers about whom I have inquired he would agree the amount he has mentioned is infinitesimal indeed. I thank him however for bringing down the return.

speechtext: Mr. S. H. KNOWLES (Winnipeg North Centre) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 9, to amend the Judges Act (salaries of judges).

subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES IN OFFICE AFTER REACHING THE AGE OF SEVENTY YEARS '
speechtext: Explain.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: SALARIES OF JUDGES IN OFFICE AFTER REACHING THE AGE OF SEVENTY YEARS '
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill would add a new subsection to section 28 of the Judges Act, which is chapter 105 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927. The authority for legislation such as that proposed in this bill is to be found in section 100 of the British North America Act.
The purpose of the proposed addition is to provide that any judge of a superior court of any province or of the Yukon territory who continues or is continued in office after attaining the age of seventy shall have his salary reduced to an amount equal to that which he would receive by way of retiring allowance if he were retired at seventy, less any sum which he may receive from a provincial government by way of other remuneration. The new salary rate will commence 100-74
when the judge attains the age of seventy years, or on the 1st day of September, 1944, whichever is the later date. In the case of a judge, appointed prior to the passing of this bill, who would not be entitled to a retiring allowance if he were to retire at the age of seventy, the operation of the act will be postponed until he is eligible for a retiring allowance.
This bill is similar to one which was passed by the House of Commons on the 10th of May, 1933, but which was rejected by the senate. Apart from the effective date, the bill is exactly the same as the one passed by this house in 1933, but for two differences. In the first place the former bill stipulated seventy-five as the age at which the provisions of that bill were to apply, whereas this bill stipulates the age of seventy. Secondly, the former bill made an exception in the case of judges not eligible for retiring allowance at the stipulated age, whether appointed before or after the passing of the bill. In this bill the same exception is provided, but only in the case of judges appointed -prior to the passing of this bill.
This bill is in line with the points made in the house by the governments of the day, both in 1927 and in 1933, relating to the judiciary. I submit that it offers a reasonable way of effecting a desirable change, pending amendment of the British North America Act,
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

2.	(a) Yes. The general conditions form M & S 1307 (capital expenditures) which are annexed as schedule "B" to order in council P C. 6284 dated July 20, 1942, contain the following provisions:
Under part II-dealing with additional equipment:
"7. Removal of additional equipment
The contractor may at any time after the lapse of twelve months from the termination of the war in which His Majesty is presently engaged, give notice in writing to the minister requiring His Majesty to remove the additional equipment from any building which is the property of the contractor or which the contractor occupies as tenant by virtue of a lease made with a lessor other than His Majesty, and upon receipt by the minister of any such notice, His Majesty shall, provided that the additional equipment in the opinion of the minister is not required for the manufacture of munitions of war or supplies in any such building, cause such additional equipment to be removed therefrom within a period of thirty days following the receipt of such notice, or within such extended period as may be reasonably required for such removal. The right herein conferred shall mutatis mu-tandis be exercisable by the contractor on behalf of any of its sub-contractors in any case where any additional equipment has been installed with the consent of His Majesty in any building which is the property of any such subcontractor or which any such sub-contractor occupies as tenant by virtue of a lease made with a lessor other than His Majesty."
Under part III-dealing with plant additions:
"10. Title to vest in His Majesty
Subject to the provisions of the agreement the plant addition, both during construction 100-74i
and after completion, shall be the property of His Majesty, provided that if the plant addition is constructed upon lands owned by the contractor, such lands shall remain the property of the contractor but if so required by His Majesty, shall be made available to His Majesty, free of charge, until five years after the cessation of hostilities in the present waT and His Majesty shall have an irrevocable option, exercisable until but not after five years after the cessation of the present war in which His Majesty is engaged, to purchase such lands at a fair and reasonable price to be determined by mutual agreement or, in default of agreement, by the exchequer court."
In cases where the extensions and additions have been built within the contractor's plant for war purposes and which are likely to interfere with the operation of the plant for civilian business, it has been agreed that within a reasonable period after the cessation of hostilities the government and the contractor will review the matter and if no satisfactory arrangement can be arrived at with respect to the disposal of the extensions and additions, the same will be removed by the government.

maintopic: WARTIME INDUSTRIAL TRANSIT AUTOMOBILE INSURANCE-BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
1.	The wartime industrial transit plan is not operated by the government. The government does not collect premiums, pay claims or bear the cost of operation. For this reason the information asked for is not available. See also the answer to question No. 4.
2.	Answered by No. 1.
3.	Answered by No. 1.
4.	The insurance coverage was developed in discussion with the provincial superintendents of insurance who were the executive of the provincial superintendents' conference. The policy settled and approved by the provincial superintendents covered
Questions

only the legal liability of the drivers to their passengers carried under the plan. The companies, however, undertook by the policies not to . raise any guest laws, and high policy limits eliminated the possibility of guest laws being raised against passengers by drivers. At the same time, the transit controller through the provincial superintendents and the representatives of the insurance companies procured from all insurers in Canada an undertaking that "ride-sharing" involving contributions from passengers would not be treated as invalidating automobile insurance coverage. This undertaking extended to all automobile insureds but it had particular application to the W.I.T. plan insurance where contributions among workmen are common. While the policy written was technically a liability policy, the pool has found it possible and desirable to pay compensation to every passenger workman injured while carried under the plan regardless of the quantity or in fact the existence of negligence on the part of the driver. In addition, the policy which strictly only covered claims of passengers approved for carriage byr a particular driver, has in practice been treated as covering in respect of any passenger workmen of the same plant or any other plant operated under the plan. The provincial superintendents later settled and approved an endorsement which adds accident coverage on each driver including an indemnity provision of up to $30 per week for 100 weeks. If reserves set up against unpaid losses are adequate, the pool has established a surplus to date, but drivers are frequently injured and occasionally killed while driving under the plan and it is expected that the combination policy may exceed a safe loss ratio. The premium, which was experimentally set at SI per car per month, remains unchanged. The expressed object of the pool is to operate as closely as possible to a five per cent margin basis with any balance of premiums allocated to a pool fund to maintain the rate level against the increased losses anticipated. The pool also intends that the experience and rate level will be reviewed again at June 30, 1944.

REDEMPTION OF WORN AND MUTILATED COINAGE
speechtext: What action, if any, has been taken to redeem smooth and mutilated Canadian coinage?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: REDEMPTION OF WORN AND MUTILATED COINAGE
speechtext:
_ Silver, nickel and bronze coin of the Dominion of Canada, which is worn smooth by natural abrasion, is redeemed by the Bank of Canada at face value. Silver, nickel and bronze coin which has been appreciably reduced in weight by any means except natural abrasion is redeemed by the Bank of Canada at a discount of 25 per cent of its face value.
The withdrawal of smooth and mutilated coinage from circulation is, in the first instance, a responsibility of the commercial banks. The procedure is to have the coins forwarded for redemption to one of the various agencies of the Bank of Canada.
It is possible that due to the shortage of subsidiary coinage caused by unprecedented demands arising out of the war, some branches [Mr. Sinclair.)
of the commercial banks have found it necessary, in order to meet public demand, to keep in circulation smooth or mutilated coins instead of withdrawing them as rapidly as prior to the outbreak of war.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence for Air
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
The hon. member
for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) asked several questions with regard to the wartime bureau of technical personnel. The questions and answers are as follows:
1.	Does the wartime bureau of technical personnel cooperate with the R.C.A.F. in the enlistment of technical personnel?
Answer:	Yes. The wartime bureau of
technical personnel cooperates fully with the R.C.A.F. In the past the bureau has supplied the R.C.A.F. with a considerable number of technical personnel for technical appointments and also, since the inception of the science student regulations, December 1, 1942, the bureau has given its consent to the enlistment as aircrew of a large number of undergraduates who have applied for consent.
2.	Are such personnel prohibited from enlisting as aircrew?
Answer:	No. Science graduates may enlist as aircrew provided they obtain the consent of the wartime bureau of technical personnel. The bureau, however, is reluctant to give its consent to a science graduate if there is an unfilled demand at the time, from the

War Appropriation-Air Services
armed forces or essential civilian employers, for men with the training or experience possessed by that graduate.
The present regulations with regard to science students apply only to those students who have graduated subsequent to December 1, 1942; neither do they apply to undergraduate science students who leave university prior to graduation. These men may enlist in any branch of the armed forces.
3.	Are they prevented from enlisting in any capacity?
Answer: No, but the conditions which apply in paragraph 2 which I have just read, are applicable in that regard also.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) asked a question with regard to the application of the order in council to Canadians serving in the R.A.F. The Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) on June 23, 1943, made the following [DOT] statement, which I think answers the hon. member:
Inquiries have been made as to whether Canadian boys, who left Canada a few years before the war to enlist in the Royal Air Force, subsequently saw active service and returned to Canada, at the time of their discharge, are eligible for benefits under the post-discharge reestablishment order (P.C. 7633).
This is the order in council which provides several of the most important measures of government assistance to ex-service men in their reestablishment problem, including vocational training, out-of-work benefit, and educational assistance.
It is the intention of the department to grant the benefits of this order in council to Canadians who serve in the R.A.F. as just described, and no additional legislation or order in council is considered necessary.
The post-discharge order provides, -with respect to members of His Majesty's forces other than Canadian forces, that they must have been domiciled in Canada at the time of their enlistment therein in the present war.
Domicile is a question of intention and of fact that cannot be divided by an arbitrary date line. Any regulation stating that those who enlisted subsequent to a particular date shall be deemed eligible might have the effect of excluding somebody who, under the present legal position, would be eligible.
The department has taken the view that any Canadian boy who left Canada two or three or even four years prior to the outbreak of war for the purpose of enlisting in His Majesty's imperial forces and who returns to Canada upon his discharge would not have forfeited his domicile for the purposes of the order.
I wish to state, therefore, that Canadian boys who left Canada a few years before the war to join H.M. imperial forces to serve in the present war, and who return to Canada upon their discharge, have not necessarily by so doing lost their domicile, and will be regarded as eligible under the order unless there be some circumstance in the individual case indicating that the applicant has actually transferred his domicile permanently out of Canada.
The hon. member for York South also asked this question: Are R.C.A.F. personnel attached to the R.A.F. and serving in India required to stay there for four years?
Present arrangements with respect to (i) aircrew personnel, (ii) R.D.F. personnel, (iii) ground crew personnel are as follows:
Aircrew personnel:	Upon completion of
each operational and non-operational or instructional tour future employment will be decided upon by the Air Officer Commanding-in-Chief, R.C.A.F. Overseas, in consultation with the appropriate R.A.F. authority. The number of such tours to be served in India before return to the United Kingdom in any particular case will depend upon the availability of replacements and operational expediencies.
Such tours of duty for aircrew personnel are as follows:
(a)	Operational: A tour of operational duty presently expressed either as a number of sorties or as a number of operational hours flown will, irrespective of the theatre of war in which the tour is served, remain as at present constituted, subject to the overriding time limitation of eighteen months or such shorter period as may be in effect in the command concerned.
(b)	Non-operational or instructional tour for ex-operational personnel: The duration of the instructional tour will be twelve months or such shorter period as may be in effect in the command concerned.
(c)	General: The tour of duty outside of Canada for R.C.A.F. aircrew personnel will not exceed three years reckoned from the date of departure from Canada until embarkation upon relief.
R.D.F. personnel: The normal tour of duty outside of Canada, including India, for R.D.F. personnel of the R.CA.F. serving with the R.A.F. shall be three years computed from the date of departure from Canada. Priority in repatriation where possible will be given to those R.D.F. personnel serving outside the United Kingdom.
Ground crew personnel: The tour of duty of R.C.A.F. ground crew attached to the R.A.F. and serving in India is indefinite, depending upon the availability of replacements and operational expediencies as may be determined from time to time by the Air Officer Commanding-in-Chief, R.C.A.F. Overseas.
The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor) asked why it was necessary to transfer the "Y" depot to Lachine.
Owing to the extreme shortage of civilian accommodation in Halifax, Nova Scotia, it was

War Appropriation-Air Services
necessary that as many service personnel as possible, living in civilian accommodation, be moved into government quarters. Personnel of the Royal Canadian Navy made up the majority of service personnel living in civilian accommodation and there was no naval accommodation available to house these personnel. Therefore, it was decided to turn over the buildings occupied by the R.C.A.F. "Y" depot to the navy and move the R.C.A.F. "Y" depot personnel to a new location. Priority was given to naval personnel in this regard as it was esential that they remain in Halifax, whereas the R.C.A.F. "Y" depot could be accommodated elsewhere with no loss in efficiency.
He also asked, was the transfer justified in view of extra cost in transportation to R.C.A.F. and personnel of the R.C.A.F. The answer is: The transfer of the R.C.A.F. "Y" depot to Lachine was justified inasmuch as Lachine, P.Q., was a more strategic location for an embarkation depot, permitting the overseas shipment of personnel from the American north Atlantic ports as well as the Canadian north Atlantic ports without increasing the travelling distance of the overseas drafts. The utilization of American north Atlantic ports was, of course, impossible prior to December 7, 1941, and hence Halifax, the largest Canadian north Atlantic port, was the most suitable location when R.C.A.F. "Y" depot was first formed prior to the entry of the United States of America into the war.
The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor) asked: Are facilities through New York as good as or better than through Halifax?
Answer: With the numerous rail lines converging on the port of New York and the extensive terminal facilities available there, that port is considered equal to Halifax for embarkation purposes.
(2)	Is New York embarkation as efficient as Halifax?
Answer: Yes; embarkations of air force personnel at New York are supervised by air force embarkation staffs and are as efficient as Halifax embarkations.
The following question was asked of the minister: Can Canadian nationals now serving in the R.A.F. as groundcrew be transferred to the Royal Canadian Air Force?
Answer: Yes, under the conditions and subject to the restrictions laid down and agreed upon by the governments of the United Kingdom and Canada as tabled in the house.
The hon. member for North Battleford (Mrs. Nielson) and the hon. leader of the opposition 
(Mr. Graydon) asked a question with regard to the pay and allowances of the members of the women's division.
Answer: (1) Responsible officers of the three services have given very full consideration to this question and they are of opinion that the principle of equal pay for equal duties is fully recognized in the present pay arrangement.
(2)	Men and women may be equally useful in the trades sphere, and indeed we recognize that they are by granting the same additional and trades pay.
(3)	It is only in the basic rates of pay that women receive four-fifths of the rate of pay for men. Service authorities do not consider that women can perform the same duties as men, because in event of enemy attack the men must man guns and meet the enemy in combat. Wherever there has been possibility ef enemy attack, the male ground personnel have been instructed in combat duties and detailed to defence posts.
(4)	In the United Kingdom, the women's forces receive approximately two-thirds of the rate of pay for men, including trades pay. We have placed our women comparatively on a much higher level of pay.
The following questions were asked with regard to aircrew messes:
(1)	Why do they eat separately?
(2)	What is ration scale compared to ground?
(3)	Size (capacity).
The answers are as follows:
(1)	Accommodation for aircrew messes, where all aircrews, regardless of rank, take certain meals together during periods of operational duty, has been established at the following units in Canada and Newfoundland (in many cases this accommodation is arranged for in existing messes): Yarmouth, Sydney, Gander, Dartmouth, Torbay, Goose Bay.
(2)	These special messes are provided for crews of squadrons that are engaged in long operational patrols. Crews of these squadrons are, by the nature of their duties, required to be absent from the units for long periods and therefore some special arrangement regarding their meals is essential. As a rule these crews, officers and other ranks, have a very early breakfast together at the unit. This provides arrangements for all personnel entitled to special rations to be messed together and centralizes the preparation of foods to be consumed aboard aircraft, as these crews take with them food for frequent light meals during the day, such as hot drinks, soups, fruit juices, sandwiches, et cetera. Frequent feedings are

War Appropriation-Air Services
recommended to delay the onset of fatigue and maintain efficiency. On their return late in the evening, after the normal supper hour at the unit is over, these crews are fatigued and hungry and are given a hearty evening meal.
(3)	Special rations have been provided for aircrew on operational duty for consumption during flight when absent from their unit during meal hours and also to provide for meals served at irregular hours in the aircrew mess. These rations include the ordinary ration normally supplied to groundcrew with the addition of increases of such items as fresh milk, fresh meat, fruit juices, sugar, tea, coffee, butter, and also includes other foods, such as canned soup, canned beef stew, cooked meats, canned vegetables and canned fruits.
(4)	Size and capacity of such messes is determined by the number of squadrons engaged in operational duties from the unit.
(5)	These messing arrangements apply only to operational units. At training stations three messes (airmen's, N.C.O.'s and officers) are in use.
The following questions were asked with regard to transportation:

(2)	What is the present situation?

The hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) asked a question with regard to R.A.F. warrant officers serving with R.CA.F. overseas stations. The answer is as follows:
R.A.F. personnel serving with R.C.A.F. overseas stations or units are paid from air ministry funds on the basis of R.A.F. regulations. It is considered that the R.A.F. would have very strong objections to personnel of their service in the United Kingdom being paid at other than R.A.F. rates, particularly in view of the invidious comparison which would arise between such personnel and other R.A.F. personnel serving at R.A.F. units in the surrounding area.
The hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) asked a question with regard to educational service in the units. The answer is lengthy. I think hon. members would like to have it on Hansard, and I shall therefore, read it:
The provision of opportunities for service personnel to continue their formal education was made in the early days of the war. The Caandian Legion educational services provided correspondence courses at high school and university level for service personnel. Tutorial classes and lectures in any subject for which there was a demand were also arranged. It was gradually realized, however, that the educational needs of service personnel could be met most adequately only if there was organized within the R.C.A.F. an educational branch. Therefore, in March, 1942, the R.C.A.F. undertook to provide education officers throughout the service. Appoint-

War Appropriation-Air Services
ment of education officers was accordingly made at all R.C.A.F. units and stations whose size warranted such action.
The R.C.A.F. educational branch now offers the following services:
Unit education officers. Almost all units of any size now have an education officer. At others there is an officer who devotes part of his time to educational duties. This applies in the case of elementary flying training schools.
The education officer on a unit or station has many duties. Among them are the following :
(a)	To advise the commanding officer on all matters relating to educational services.
(b)	To ascertain the educational needs of all personnel on the unit and advise such personnel with regard to educational facilities.
(c)	To make appropriate recommendations regarding the educational qualifications of all personnel who desire to remuster to aircrew. To administer the necessary classification tests in this connection.
(d)	To organize educational courses, trade improvement classes, progress of war study and tutorial classes as may be necessary.
(e)	To advise personnel with regard to educational facilities available through the Canadian Legion educational services and to supervise all examinations in connection with educational activities on a unit.
(f)	To give progress of war lectures to aircrew trainees in accordance with the syllabi of training.
(g)	To organize the station library.
(h)	To assist the commanding officer in organizing discussion and study groups in current affairs and progress of war.
Pre-aircrew education. At most units where there is an education officer, ground personnel who desire to remuster to aircrew and who lack the required educational qualifications are given the necessary courses organized on the unit by the education officer. To date nearly 11,000 airmen have remustered to aircrew.
A large number of personnel who enlist for aircrew duties are qualified in all respects except education. Pre-aircrew training schools have therefore been organized under the war emergency training plan at fifteen points across the dominion for these aircrew trainees. These schools are operated by the dominion Department of Labour and the educational services of the R.C.A.F. have complete responsibility for direction and supervision of training. The schools give courses ranging from six to sixteen weeks and give preliminary training to prospective air gunners, wireless air gunners,

pilots, navigators, flight engineers, air observers, air bombers. The subjects studied are science, mathematics, English, signals, aircraft recognition, drill and P.T. and progress of war.
In addition to these fifteen pre-aircrew W.E.T.P. schools there are eight university R.C.A.F. detachments across the dominion. The courses offered vary from six to sixteen weeks in length according to the aircrew category of the trainee. The subjects studied are the same as in W.E.T.P. schools.
To date 22,604 aircrew trainees have graduated from W.E.T.P. schools and pre-aircrew education detachments.
Progress of war. It is recognized nowadays that modern mechanized warfare requires not only technical training and skill but also a high standard of general information and intelligence. The strains of modern warfare can best be endured by men who know actually what they are fighting for and what they are fighting against. To meet this need the R.C.A.F. has organized a progress of war programme which consists of two main types of activities:
(a)	There is a programme of progress of war lectures and discussion for pre-aircrew and aircrew trainees. Definite training time is allotted and the programme to be followed1 is outlined in the various training syllabi. Progress of war lectures in training time are included in the syllabi for pre-aircrew, I.T.S., E.F.T.S., S.F.T.S., air gunner and navigation schools.
(b)	Discussion groups and lectures are organized for all personnel. The organization of discussion groups for all officers, airmen and airwomen at all R.C.A.F. units and stations is the responsibility of commanding officers.
(c)	Basic material for discussion groups is provided in the publication Canadian Affairs which is published twice monthly by the wartime information board1 in cooperation with the directors of education of the three armed services. It is distributed in Canada and overseas. The aim of Canadian Affairs is to keep service personnel informed with regard to significant social and economic developments in Canada with special attention to the effects of the war. Questions for discussion and comment have been included and a resume of news of the home front has been given in each issue.
In connection with progress of war activities, every effort is made to employ films to the best advantage. Film libraries are established and all commands and the command education officer is responsible for organizing film circuits for all units. The selection of suitable films dealing with the background

War Appropriation-Air Services
of progress of war is made at air force headquarters.
The object of the discussion groups scheme is to make all ranks of the R.C.A.F. better acquainted with the high ideals for which the war is being fought; with the important and responsible part which they must play in order to hasten the day of victory and with the possibilities whicn the post-war work holds for the ordinary man and woman; in a word, to make them more effective members of the air force community to-day and better citizens of the world to-morrow. The scheme should thus contribute materially to the general keenness and efficiency of the service and should counteract any tendency towards slackness or apathy which there may be, particularly among those whose duties are monotonous or seemingly unconnected with active operations against the enemy.
Trade improvement. The technical efficiency of all personnel in ground trades is a matter of vital concern to the service. For this reason trade tests are given at regular intervals, to facilitate advancement and correct grouping of members of the service. It is the duty of the education officer on the station to organize classes for ground crew personnel who have not reached their maximum trade proficiency. The educational services of the R.C.A.F. have provided manuals for students and instructors covering various trades in order that trade improvement classes may be organized in the most effective manner. The best teaching techniques are carefully outlined and every effort is made to organize instruction and material in such a manner that the student and instructor may derive the most benefit. Manuals have already been issued in such trades as aero-engine mechanics, airframe mechanics, equipment assistant, clerks, wireless mechanics and wireless operator, motor mechanics (mechanical transport), i manual for seamen, welders and metal workers, and machinists.
Additional manuals are prepared in other trades as the need for them becomes apparent. Trade improvement classes have contributed materially to the high efficiency of R.C.A.F. ground personnel.
Self-improvement classes. This term covers a great variety of educational activities. There are' service personnel who wish to use their spare time for the improvement of their academic standing. Such personnel may enroll for matriculation or university, classes in nearby educational institutions. The latest educational reports from stations indicate that personnel are studying such subjects as mathematics, history, French, Spanish, German,
Russian, economics, psychology, chemistry and bacteriology. This work is carried out under the necessary arrangements with the educational institutions. In many cases he also gives tutorial assistance and organizes station classes in academic subjects.
Other personnel are interested in the following commercial courses such as typing, shorthand, and bookkeeping. Here again the classes may be organized on the station or the personnel may enroll at nearby commercial schools.
Still others are interested in improving their technical knowledge and ability. Arrangements have been made for these to enroll in technical schools in the vicinity of their units in order to follow courses in such subjects as welding, carpentry, electricity, motor mechanics, plastics, diesel engineering, mechanical drawing and so on.
Unit education officers are giving particular attention to the provision of worth-while educational activities for W.D. personnel and at many stations throughout Canada W.D. personnel are taking part in courses such as the following: Cooking and home making) clothing and home management; art; dramatics; music and singing; current events group; language groups.
In addition to the more formal courses outlined above various handicraft groups are being organized on the stations. This programme has been particularly valuable from the point of view of morale and of selfimprovement.
At present there are well over 7,000 personnel who are making constructive use of their spare time in academic, business or technical courses or in participating in handicraft work or in some other similar line of activity.	.
Correspondence courses. Unit education officers have enrolled over 10,000 personnel in correspondence courses at high school and university level who desire to continue their formal education. The correspondence course work of these personnel is often supplemented by the organization of tutorial classes at units.
Libraries. Station libraries are proving to be a very necessary supplement to the various educational activities of the units. The unit education officer is chiefly responsible for the organization of station libraries.
The educational services of the R.C.A.F. are endeavouring to meet the following objectives:
(a) To advance the skill and raise the technical efficiency of those who are aiready engaged in a particular trade in the service.

War Appropriation-Air Services
(b)	to assist those who wish to learn a new trade, or fit themselves for a better post-war vocation.
(c)	to assist those who wish to continue their general or professional education.
(d)	To promote intelligent interest in the war.
To the extent that the above objectives are met, R.C.A.F. personnel will be the better equipped to carry out their duties, in the service, and as citizens in time of peace.
A course in English, twelve to sixteen weeks duration, is provided at No. 1 manning depot, Toronto, for French-Canadian trainees, to give them greater facility in the use of the English language and thus enable them to take the subsequent service courses of training. In the course of English emphasis is placed on the technical vocabulary of the various ground and aircrew trades. The school of English also provides the trainees with a course in progress of war and current events.
To date over 7,000 French-Canadian trainees have graduated from the school of English.
No. 1 ground instructor's school was organized in August, 1943, for the training of ground instructors in classroom techniques. Over 300 ground school instructors have already taken the course, which is of three weeks' duration, and it is considered that this school has contributed materially to the efficiency of ground school instruction at training schools.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I do not think that is a satisfactory answer to my question about R.A.F. personnel. I asked whether the government had given consideration to paying R.A.F. personnel who are serving with R.C.A.F. squadrons at R.C.A.F. rates of pay. The answer I got was that it was considered that the R.A.F. would think it invidious to have R.A.F. personnel in Canadian squadrons drawing more than their personnel with RA.F. squadrons. I suggest it is not as invidious a position as that of the R.A.F. squadron leader who commands a Canadian squadron and who has to learn tnat tne commander of the squadron receives less than the flight-lieutenant, less than the flying officer, less than the pilot officer, less than the flight-sergeant pilot, and just a little more than the sergeant pilot. The Royal Navy does not think it invidious to let the Royal Canadian Navy pay Royal Navy personnel on Canadian ships at Canadian rates. Has the R.C.A.F. suggested directly to the R.A.F. that, since they are taking the full cost of R.C.A.F. squadrons, they are willing to pay these R.A.F. personnel at R.C.A.F. rates of pay?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I did not suggest it directly. I did mention it in the course of conversations, but I would not be particularly keen to do it at the present time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: The question is not very important so far as Canadians in the R.A.F. are concerned, because they are going to be transferred. But my appeal, made a few days ago, was one for the airmen. We are using these airmen. We are taking them on, because they are good key men. Why should these two warrant officers in the squadron about which I spoke lead that crew at the pay of a corporal? I do not like to hold up the other services as a model for my own service, but in this instance I believe the Royal Canadian Navy is to be commended upon accepting these chaps as Canadians.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: My hon. friend will remember that practically all the R.A.F. men serving in Canada are paid at R.C.A.F. rates of pay.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I understand that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Before the war a number of our boys went overseas and joined the R.A.F. At the present time they are not considered eligible for the Canadian volunteer medal. They feel they are slighted in that regard, and that they should be entitled to it. Has the minister considered the point?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: This is the first time I have heard of it, but I shall be glad to look into it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I
have talked with a number of those boys, and have received a number of letters. This is a paragraph from one:
It seems very unfair to me that fellows like myself who went overseas before the war to join the British service are not considered as Canadians and volunteers and are therefore not eligible for the Canadian volunteer medal.
He goes on to say:
I hope you will urge for some similar medal for Canadians. And there are many who volunteered for service before the war when things looked very black at the time of Munich. In our town alone there were-
A number of boys-[DOT]
-who joined the RA.F. before the war.
He states also that those who joined the Royal Navy and the British army should be considered. There is some merit in that suggestion.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
My understanding is-and
frankly, I speak subject to correction, because I do not know much about it-that the volunteer medal is entirely a Canadian medal. I have some doubt as to whether a man serving in another force would be entitled

War Appropriation-Air Services
to put it up. However, I am not sure about that. Perhaps the hon. member for Royal would know more about that than I.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Could there not be another kind of medal for those boys, similar to the Canadian volunteer medal?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I would have some difficulty in explaining how the Canadian government could strike a medal for the use of people serving in other forces. But if it can be done, I would have no objection.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: These boys are still Canadians.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I understand that; but the question with me is whether the other services would allow them to put it up. However, I do not mind looking into the matter.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Does the minister not think the suggestion has some merit?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: So far as I am concerned it does not matter to me at all. I shall look into it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: All Canadians in the R.A.F. will get the general service medal, 1939-43, from the British government, which they would not have got had they stayed in Canada. Most of them are prouder of the fact that they wear the Canada badge on their shoulders than they are of the service medal. That shows that they are Canadians.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I
think they would also like to have the volunteer medal.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I believe it was stated that it was considered invidious for Canadian airmen in the R.A.F. to receive more pay than R.A.F. personnel received. My understanding is that we are sending about 1,500 army officers to the British army, and that they are to receive Canadian pay. Frankly I do not see how it would be more invidious for the airmen to receive such pay than for the army. I believe there should be some coordination between the air force, the army and the navy in matters of this kind; if one receives a certain rate of pay, they should all receive the comparative rates.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
These are men who are in the R.A.F., and who now have the opportunity to transfer, if they like, under certain circumstances. If they prefer to stay in another service, and then ask us to pay them in another service, I think my friends in the treasury might object. On the other hand the men about whom the hon. member for Royal has spoken are Canadians who have been lent
to the imperial army, in the same way as a good many R.C.A.F. men have been lent to the R.A.F. Canada pays their full salary, of course.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: The fighting, it seems to me, is the same, and the service is the same. No doubt the responsibilities these men have taken are the same. Those are factors which should be taken into consideration perhaps more than some which have been mentioned by the minister.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I asked a question on Friday respecting Canadian nationals in the R.A.F. subject to income tax.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I remember that question. I was astonished when my hon. friend stated in the house that the Americans-or perhaps it was not my hon. friend who said it-who had transferred from the R.A.F. back to the American force were reimbursed the amount of the income tax they had paid into the treasury of Great Britain. My hon. friend was not quite clear as to whether the reimbursement was made by the American government or the British government. I learned afterwards-I believe from the hon. member for Vancouver North-that the British government had done it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: When they joined they were promised that it would not be deducted. They were promised that in America before they went to England.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I see; that is another story. I am informed there has been no approach made by the British treasury to repay those Canadians any income tax they may have paid the British treasury. That is as far as I have got. It will involve communication with the other side to get further information. If it is not a fact that the British government are going to consider reimbursing these men, then that will involve a diplomatic approach on my part to our treasury.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: What I am concerned about is whether the minister's department intends to make that representation. My information on the United States angle-I do not intend to elaborate this-comes from Canadian nationals in the R.A.F., and I think it is authentic.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I do not know just how it was worked, whether the United States government reimburse these men for income tax paid to the British treasury or whether, as the hon. member for Vancouver North says, the arrangement was that where Americans enlisted in the R.A.F. they were not to be

War Appropriation-Air Services
subject to British income tax. If that is a fact, naturally the British treasury would reimburse them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Is the minister or his parliamentary assistant in a position to give us some information with regard to retirement of members of the permanent R.C.A.F.? I notice the minister answered a question asked by the hon. member for Vancouver North, but I do not know just what information was given. I asked a question the other evening in connection with the retirement of high ranking officers. I wanted to know what rank they held when retired, what rank they held at the beginning of the war, what pension is being paid, some indication of the ages of these men and whether they are capable of carrying on similar work or whether their health is so much impaired that they would be of no further service.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Nine permanent officers have been or are being retired since the beginning of the war. I may say that the retirements were not based on health.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: What were their ages?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Their ages ran around fifty years. In the statement I gave I said it was proposed to retire men who were comparatively young. As I said, there is a thick ceiling of comparatively young men at the top. Through no fault of their own, these men have not been able to see active service, and it was hoped that men who had seen active service would gradually get to the top as they returned from overseas. I do not mean that men necessarily will be retired in order of age, that a man of fifty-one or fifty-two years of age who is an air vice marshal will be retired and a man of forty-nine years of age take his place. It may be that a man of fifty-nine years of age will be retired before a man of fifty-two years of age, not necessarily because his services are not satisfactory but- I think the country will agree with me in this [DOT]-because it is imperative that we show these young men that there is a way through this ceiling by which they can get to the top. That is the general policy.
The pensions they receive are quite reasonable amounts. I have not the details, but they run from $4,500 to $5,500 per year. These ire contributory pensions under the Militia Pension Act, which has been in effect for some thirty or forty years. There is no great hardship involved in retiring these men, although my hon. friend has raised a point in that connection. For some considerable time the treasury mar have to pay fairly

high pensions, but I do not think the air force should be asked to keep these men in positions where younger men will not be able to come forward. It is part of the pension scheme under which they enlisted. It may be a little expensive for the country, but I suppose the country will have to put up with it for the good of the service generally.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: It all depends upon how rapid their promotion was during the last four years.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Promotion was exceedingly rapid, but you cannot have the expansion of a force from 4,000 to 200,000 without having rapid promotions. You must give men ranks called for by their increased responsibilities. A man who in peace time may have been in charge of ten or twenty men, would probably be in charge of from 2,000 to 3,000 men now. A man who was in charge of an equipment depot of $100,000 worth of goods, will now be dealing with an equipment depot with $100,000,000 worth of goods. Responsibilities increased as we expanded, and these men necessarily obtained promotions. As I said in my statement, rapid expansion means rapid promotion, rapid promotion brings its own penalty of early retirement.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Does the same principle apply to the army and navy?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I understand the army beat me to it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Good for them. It is the first time they have done it.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: The Minister of National Defence stated that in the house. They have been doing it for eight or ten months.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Could the minister give us any information as to how many high ranking officers over the age of fifty-five years have been retired?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Very few; I do not suppose there would be ten. I have a copy of the answer that was given to-day. The question asked was:
How many officers of the R.C.A.F. of air rank have been retired since September 10. 1939. (a) of the permanent force; (b) of the auxiliary force; (c) of the special reserve?
The answer given was:
(i)	One officer of the permanent force.
(ii)	Three permanent force officers presently on retirement leave-two retirements effective in June and one in July of this year.
(iii)	Five permanent force officers whose retirements have been authorized but not yet promulgated.
There seems to be an idea that it is only permanent force officers who are to be retired, and that idea seems about to be made into a

War Appropriation-Air Services
grievance. In addition to the permanent force officers, there was a large number of officers who entered the force at the beginning of the war. These were men of considerable experience in business and the professions; they were lawyers, engineers and so on. Some of these men have risen rapidly, but few of them are receiving the salaries which they would have enjoyed in civil life. Some came from prominent positions in the business world. These men have done a wonderful job, as the hon. member for Spadina has stated. They have been doing administrative work, since they were too old to go overseas to fight in squadrons. Early in my administration I passed regulations by which no one of aircrew age and fitness could enter the air force as an administrative officer. That is to say, if a man was under thirty-two years of age, no matter what his experience may have been as a lawyer or in any other profession-the exception was the medical profession-he could not get a commission. Therefore we had these men of experience in business who became administrative officers, and they have done a marvellous job in the expansion of our force. No one can say that their work has not been as patriotic and as helpful as that of other men in our own force or in other forces. They have now trained younger men to take their jobs, perhaps men who were in the permanent force and who are going to continue in the service after the war. I should like to state publicly that if any of these men feel that they would like to return to their occupations in civilian life, unless they are essential key men I will put no obstacle in the way of their retirement. Already that has gone forth through the services and quite a few officers, some N.C.O.'s in the higher categories whose firms require their services, are asking that they be allowed to retire. We are allowing them to do so and thanking them for the great services they have rendered.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Do they receive any retiring allowance?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: They will get the rehabilitation grant and whatever war service gratuity is given, of course.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Even for those who retire voluntarily?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I am not quite sure that that point has been straightened out as yet.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: The army does not do it.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: We do not do it yet, but I think it will be arranged that we shall, very shortly.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I understand that anybody in the air force who is seriously wounded and sent back to hospital in Canada gets the pay of his rank until he is either sent back to duty or discharged to civilian life.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: If he is discharged to Pensions and Health, he comes under Pensions and Health regulations.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: The air force has the same regulations as the army in that matter?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Absolutely.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: On comparing the typewritten list of probable cash requirements for 1943-44 and estimated requirements for 1944-45, with the details for air services given on page 394 of Hansard of February 11, 1944, under the war appropriation, I find that the figures of probable expenditure for 1944-45 on the typewritten list and in Hansard tally, but that the figures on the typewritten list of probable expenditures for 1943-44 are not in any particular similar to those given on page 394 of Hansard, the difference amounting in the aggregate to about $60,000,000.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I think I know the reason, but I will have the officers of the department come down to help me explain. There was a revision of the estimates as first brought down. I am not sure whether that came between February 11 and February 25, but I shall be glad to have the officers look into it, and then answer my hon. friend.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
What is the policy of the government with regard to the use of the Royal Canadian Air Force in the war against Japan? There has been very little said on that subject in the discussion of these estimates. I notice that on March 2 the minister said, at page 1067 of Hansard:
There would be the problem of shifting personnel from one theatre of war to another when we go toward the Japanese theatre and so on.
It would be interesting if the minister would tell the committee whether the air war on the Pacific so far as Canada is concerned is to be a defensive war until Germany is beaten, or whether there is some idea in mind of Canada taking part in the air war there in the meantime. I should think it would be wise to give at least some of our airmen training in fighting against the Japanese. Would the minister explain the situation?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Order. We have passed item 1, on which a general discussion was allowed, and we are now on item 2, pay and allowances.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I will answer the question anyway, Mr. Chairman.

War Appropriation-Air Services

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the men on the Pacific coast will have to be paid, so that I think my question is pertinent. This item is for pay and allowances.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Canada will be in the war
against Japan until the very end. I am no strategist and cannot tell my hon. friend just what part we are going to take in the war on the Pacific, but we are going to shift from the European, theatre to where we can do the most harm against Japan at the proper time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Are steps being taken to
give our airmen training in the warfare against Japan?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Steps are being considered
along those lines, if that will satisfy my hon. friend.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
The minister on March 2
asked for suggestions with regard to what should be done towards helping our airmen take their places in civilian life. It just so happened that over the week-end one or two airmen were speaking with, me and made certain suggestions. They said that even instructors on the stations in Canada have very little information about the government's rehabilitation plans. We all know that certain, publications have been issued giving a summary of what is proposed, but apparently these are not being distributed1 on the stations at all. These lads suggested that it would be very helpful if such publications were distributed., and if the men on the stations were asked for their suggestions, as they are the ones most vitally concerned, and apparently have been giving great thought to this matter. It would be helpful if they knew just what the government's plans are.
Another suggestion was that some attempt should be made to find out how many of the airmen would be willing to serve in the air force after the war; that is, to join the permanent air force. Apparently quite a few would be glad to do so, but I am told that no attempt has been made to find out just what proportion would like to do that. Inquiry should also be made as to how many would be willing to serve for six months, say, or a year, after the termination of hostilities, the understanding being that they would not thereby lose their privilege of taking vocational or university training once they had been discharged'. These lads seemed to think that it would be very helpful if the minister could get that information. I notice that in the committee on reconstruction and reestablishment the suggestion was made on February 23 that there would be from 135,000 to 150,000 men in the armed services, including munitions
'Mr. Power.]
and equipment factory workers, after the war. I do not know whether the air force have made a rough estimate of how many will be required in that service, but it looks as though the number will be quite large. I think it would be well worth while for the minister to have inquiries made among his air force personnel to find out what proportion are interested in staying in the force.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Replying to my hon. friend's first question with regard to rehabilitation, as he knows, that is a matter for Pensions and National Health. I understand that Pensions and National Health have set up a public relations office and that they are now in the process of distributing as widely as possible all the information dealing with rehabilitation to civilian life.
Iq reply to the second question, one at least of our service papers, Wings, has been giving explanations of the rehabilitation programme. I have a copy here of an article in. Wings, headed "Fighting for the Future. What do I do when the war is won?" This is in Wings of March. I know there was something in the issue of February, and also, I believe, in that of January, about return to "civvies." The Minister of Pensions and National Health says that about 100,000 copies of this little blue book were distributed1.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Are they distributed among the forces?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Among the forces overseas, yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: And in Canada also?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: If I may answer the question, a new one is being got ready and will be sent to all next of kin in Canada. It is a little more comprehensive than the other.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
In one of our service papers -I think, Contact, published at Trenton- there was a kind of Gallup poll as to what the boys wanted to do after the war, and I am told that fifty per cent thought they would like to stay in the service. So that to the extent of the Gallup poll, at least, they have been consulted. As to what the strength of the air force will be after the war, as my hon. friend knows, we are studying the matter, 'but so many factors enter into the question of the strength and nature of the armed forces of Canada after the war that I should be reluctant to make any pronouncement. I know that we shall keep a certain number for the occupational phase of Europe, a number for the policing of Europe if Canada decides to participate in it, and a large number will remain in Europe,

War Appropriation-Air Services
or wherever they may be, for quite a while after the Germans fold up, because there will not be shipping to bring them back. That will be one of our troubles. I do not think there is any prospect of an extremely hasty demobilization, at least of the people overseas.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Would it be wise to establish more operational-training units in Canada than there are at the present time? Apparently a good deal of that work is done in Great Britain, and the suggestion has been made that it might very well be done in Canada.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: On various occasions we have thought of it, and we are doing some, but our great difficulty has been to get operational aircraft for operational training units, because all this class of aircraft is wanted directly for fighting the enemy. As ray hon. friend knows, we have several operational training units in Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
What policy is
followed in the selection of training personnel? The minister has stated that some of the senior administrative officers are being retired to make room for younger officers who are coming along. Is any policy of that nature in effect for the selection of training personnel in this country?-as, when a class graduates, so many go overseas, so many are selected for training. Is there at this stage of the war any policy under which those who have had actual experience in foreign lands have the opportuuity of coming back as training officers? If so, what is the policy?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
That gives me an opportunity to answer the leader of the opposition. In operational training units, instructors must be men who have had operational experience- actual experience in contact with the enemy. In our arrangement with the United Kingdom government in 1942, when we decided to open operational training units here, we asked that all those who were sent here as instructors of our operational units should be Canadians, and they have to a certain extent followed out that policy; but that, also, has its difficult side. Some who come back here to our operational training units will in due course go to training units which are not operational. But we have made arrangements whereby most of the operational training units are up close to the front line. We shall never be able to get away from that. As a man returns from his first operational tour he is sent back for a tour in an operational training unit, because they want to use his very latest experience in the front line. The result is that a good many of our
Canadians as soon as they finish their operational tour must do a tour of what is called non-operational work, that is in an operational training unit, but it keeps them overseas a very long time before they return here. We have recently made an arrangement with the United Kingdom government whereby we shall retain in England, in the east, or in whatever theatre we maye be operating, a number of men who have done their operational work, their actual fighting operations, to work as instructors in operational training units, the number to be in proportion to the number of men we actually have in the front line of operations. Until recently the United Kingdom government just kept them Now we have reached a compromise whereby they will do their one tour of operations, one tour of instruction in operational training units, and then return to Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: There is no such policy in mind for the schools in Canada other than the operational schools?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: There is for the schools; but because these men are latest from the scene of operations, they must, after they have done their operational tour, go to an operational training school before they come back to another school. That is the general policy followed, and that is the policy we have agreed to.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
And there is as yet a
lack of those officers for other schools in this country?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Yes, but as soon as we get them back they will have first choice of any instructional work. I may say that all of them do not like it. Even those who come back now are offered instructional work as soon as they get here.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Have any of the Royal
Canadian Air Force been trained in transport planes and the transporting of troops by air?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: We are opening a transport O.T.U. next month in Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Would the minister give us some figures with regard to the number of non-commissioned officers, warrant officers and commissioned ranks who are prisoners of war, and what the policy of the department is with regard to granting promotions to these men after they are prisoners of war? Is there any difference in automatic promotions as between warrant officers and N.C.O.'s and commissioned ranks?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I am not sure I have that information here. I have not got it broken down. The total number of officer prisoners

War Appropriation-Air Services
of war appears to be 363, and the total number of N.C.O.'s, 847. I know that we have a policy developed on that, and I know the general lines of it, but I should prefer, if my hon. friend will wait until this evening, to give him then the policy more, specifically.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
When the minister gives that information will he also inform the committee as to the method of granting commissions? We have discussed this in previous years under the estimates of the Department of National Defence. I was one of those who suggested that all members of aircrew should be commissioned-not that I believe in that in principle, but because so many commissions had been granted that I felt, as did others, that there should be a general granting of commissions to members of aircrew.
