If I remember correctly the method adopted in Canada in 1940 was to grant commissions to one-third of those who graduated and subsequently to grant commissions to seventeen per cent more when they got overseas; that is to say, fifty per cent of each class graduating in Canada eventually received commissions. In 1942 there was a change made, if I remember correctly, and all pilots, observers, navigators and air gunners who were considered suitable according to the standards of the government of Canada, and who were recommended by their commanding officers, were commissioned. I think the standard set in Canada was sixty per cent for each subject and seventy per cent in all during training operations; that is to say, a young man taking a course as a pilot in Canada would have to receive sixty per cent in each subject and seventy per cent on his total in order to get a commission on graduation. I approve that method because it sets a standard toward which a man can strive while he is taking his training. But I do not think those who do not succeed in reaching that standard during their training should be deprived of ever getting a commission. I think they should still be considered as worthy of commissions after they have proven themselves in the air. I believe they should still be allowed to strive for a commission, and I hope that when the minister replies he will tell the committee whether opportunity is given to those who do not attain to sixty per cent or seventy per cent during their training to obtain commissions later on.
Another matter I should like to bring to the minister's attention is the question which was raised by the hol>
member who spoke with regard to granting commissions before I rose to speak. I refer t*,. the question of men who are taken prisoners. Do the enemy recognize commissions which are granted after

a man has been taken prisoner? Suppose he were not gazetted until some time after he had been forced down in enemy country, is the commission then recognized? As far as I am concerned I should like to think that all men who fly over enemy territory are commissioned, because without doubt they receive better treatment as officers than as noncommissioned officers.
The hon. member for Vancouver North, speaking the other day from his .very wide experience, suggested that there should be a mess where all aircrew should dine and live together. I understood that that was so when they were in actual operations. He referred to certain messes in North Africa. I approve of that. I think it is only fair, but it does not meet the objection with regard to airmen who are forced down over enemy territory. They have not a common mess with officers who are prisoners of war. Nor does it meet the objection with regard to young men who have flown as sergeants or warrant officers probably on many, many occasions over enemy territory and who when they return to Canada are still non-commissioned officers and are not admitted to officers' messes. As long as there are two ranks, the non-commissioned officer and the officer, in aircrew, then I think we should extend the principle of a common mess where they can all live. It does not seem right that a young man who is a sergeant and has command of a plant when it is in the air,-and in the same plane there may be a commissioned officer, who must take his orders from the sergeant while the plane is in the air-must, as soon as the plane comes to the ground, walk out after the officer and go to his own mess while the officer goes to his. They do not associate. I hope that the minister will be able to tell us that commissions are being granted to these men who in training do not get the standing required. I hope he will tell us that commissions are being granted to them after they have proven themselves to be officer material, after they have proven themselves to be good flyers, after they have had a number of operations over enemy territory.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: The answer to the last question, of course, is yes. There is no bar to any man getting a commission. He may not get it immediately if he does not pass the required test, but he is certainly encouraged to proceed to a commission, to carry on useful work with every hope that he will obtain a commission even if he does not get it on graduation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Are any Royal Canadian
Air Force officers being seconded for duty

War Appropriation-Air Sermces
with the military governments in occupied countries. I believe in that way some of those men, who would otherwise be retired, may render further useful service to Canada.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
We have some following
courses now, not very many.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
It is open to air force
officers.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Are pensions paid to the wives and families of flying instructors killed in Canada?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I think Captain Balfour, Miinster for Air in Great Britain, said the other day that one-third of the fleet air arm was trained in the United States. Are we training any men for the fleet air arm?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Yes; we have two elementary and two service flying training schools training for the fleet air arm in Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: We are not sending any of our men down to the United States?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: These are.all men who come here from the British admiralty under some kind of a R.A.F. contract. In other words, the R.A.F. have handed over part of their schools to the admiralty to train men for the fleet air arm. We deal with air ministry only.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Are there any specific
limits to the operational tours?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
In answer to my hon.
friend-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
How flexible is the
arrangement?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I would prefer not to give it because it has been kept more or less as a secret.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: That is all right.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: It is a secret that everybody on operations knows. It differs. The Americans have one criterion. There is one involving sorties in the bomber command. It is hours flown in the coastal command, and so on. It is a complicated matter, but it has been always marked "secret". I do not think there is any very great secret about it, but because it is marked "secret" when it comes to me I would prefer not to make it public in the committee.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I presume that when
R.C.A.F. personnel fly in R.A.F. units, the planes are provided by the unit?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I should like to endorse what the hon. member for Brantford City has said regarding commissions. He will remember that when we were in Great Britain over two years ago. we were approached by a group of young officers who pointed out to us how ridiculous it was that they were flying every day with non-commissioned officers and that as soon as they arrived at the bomber station they had to go to two different messes. The minister will remember that we made representations in this regard when we reached London, and I think, as a matter of fact, we made representations in this house also. I just wish to lend my support to the expressions that have been' uttered in this house again this year along these lines.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I can report progress in the commissioning; we are getting ahead much better than we were. Offhand I can say that so far, out of some 32,000 who hold commissions in the air force, 25,971 persons have been commissioned from the ranks, which is not bad.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: How many officers are there in the air force altogether?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
About thirty-two thousand. As hon. members know, when we started this training plan the procedure first followed was that the top thirty-three per cent of the graduating class obtained commissions, and that seventeen per cent more were to obtain commissions overseas. The first trouble that developed was that we had great difficulty in finding that other seventeen per cent, so that in the 1942 agreement with the United Kingdom we made arrangements under which these men could themselves apply to their commanding officers, and if their commanding officers did not agree that they were commis-sionable still they could go on and eventually wind up before a board at Canadian headquarters, where the standards of these men for commissioning would be judged by Canadians.
Then we thought the quota system was not satisfactory and we instituted the merit system, under which the number of points a man obtained on graduation would count, that number being sixty in each subject and seventy over all. That developed a far greater number of commissions than the quota system; in fact, in some classes it went up to eighty per cent, while in others it went down to twenty or thirty per cent, depending upon the calibre of the class; but no longer did it depend upon a certain quota. Then we ran into difficulties with the boys overseas who had not received their commissions. They
War Appropriation-Air Services

asked how it was that a lad just graduated would come over as an officer while a fellow who had been there for two years had not received his commission. That had the salutary effect of making us try to speed up the commissioning overseas, and I think we have been fairly successful in catching up with the nacklog. There may be some who are still ost somewhere in the blue, or whose immediate commanding officers do not as yet understand the procedure. It has come to my notice that certain of our own lads who are isolated in R.A.F. units would make application and ask that their application be sent or to Canadian headquarters, but it took a long time for those applications to get there if they ever did get through. I must say that whenever we called the attention of air ministry to the matter they did not hesitate a bit in hauling their own people over the coals. That was largely because the commanding officer perhaps had never been made familiar with the agreement entered into between the United Kingdom and ourselves. I do not put it down to any ill-will at all; as far as I have been able to ascertain, now at any rate there is the best of good will prevailing between the two services. However, it is very difficult for a squadron leader in Burma or India or the middle east to know everything that is undertaken by way of agreement between the two governments. So that a large number-I do not know how many, but at least some-of our men have not as yet had their applications go through.
That is the number one backlog; that was the important thing we were trying to clean jp, and I think we have cleaned it up fairly well. Then we applied the 60-60-70 ratio to all those who had graduated, no matter where they were, prisoners of war or anything else. We just looked over their marks, and if we found that they came within this ratio we promptly commissioned them wherever they were. That caused a little trouble for a while, too, but that has been cleaned up. So that the commissioning is on a pretty fair basis at the present time, though the ultimate for which a good many of us had hoped, namely, that everybody would be commissioned, has not as yet been reached.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: That is, all aircrew.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Yes; but I would be deterred from putting that into effect at the moment because it would be so difficult. If we were to say now that everyone would be commissioned on graduation we would still have that backlog of boys who have done good service [Mr. Power.}
overseas, whom we have not been able to find and whom perhaps we could not commission; or perhaps we might have some who had done very good service but had deteriorated since then so that we could not by any means give commissions to them. Therefore I think we shall have to proceed as we have for the past six months, with a broader and more generous commissioning policy, and an agreement, firmly confirmed, with the United Kingdom covering all categories of aircrew, not only pilots, bombers and navigators, whereby the United Kingdom government definitely agree that commissioning is a matter for the Canadian government alone, and that this government shall commission according to its own standards and irrespective of those of any other nation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: What is the percentage of aircrew with Canadian squadrons in Britain who are commissioned?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I may be giving information from which, by adding or subtracting, somebody may find out something of value to the enemy; but as I figured it the last time I looked at it, it was about two to one for pilots, about the same for navigators, and about one to one for air bombers. Of course gunners are away below that; only five per cent were granted commissions on graduation. We have thousands of them over there whose cases we are now reviewing, trying to bring them up. Then wireless operator air gunners were only allowed ten per cent on graduation, with another ten per cent to be commissioned for service in the field.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Order. I believe the present discussion should come under item 13, which covers the maintenance of overseas squadrons. I must remind the committee again that we are now on item 2, which covers pay and allowances.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: The pay and allowances for N.C.O.'s and officers are different.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I think it is still pay and allowances, Mr. Chairman; it is all one to me whether I answer the question now or later. I have the ratio of officers to otheT ranks. Overseas the ratio is two officers to five other ranks in the R.C.A.F. squadrons; I am not talking about our men in the R.A.F., because I have not that information. In the Canadian squadrons, among aircrew, there are six officers to five N.C.O.'s, showing that we have made a great advance in commissioning. In the ground-crew there is one officer to thirteen other ranks, and the over-all ratio is four officers to nine other ranks.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
These figures scarcely seem to bear out the statement just made

War Appropriation-Air Services
by the minister in regard to prisoners of war, where I think he said there were 362 commissioned officers and 847 N.C.O.'s.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Of course a good many of these N.C.O.'s were taken prisoner some time ago. That would not be the very latest report.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Then could the minister give us the cost of training a wireless air gunner and the cost of training an air bomber?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: We have not a recent figure, I am told, because of a change in the syllabus. I am instructed that it has been altered so many times that it would not be fair to give any kind of figure.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Could
the minister tell the committee whether enemy governments recognize commissions that are granted after N.C.O.'s have been taken prisoner?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Perhaps I can say yes to that now. To the same inquiry I was not in a position to make that answer last year. However now I know they are doing it. But how- quickly that recognition is given, and what steps are taken to move N.C.O.'s who become officers from an N.C.O. camp to an officers' camp, I am unable to 6ay.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I should like to ask some questions respecting one or two classes of people who have been associated with the air force. 1 have in mind, first, those young Canadians who, both before and during the war, wanted to join the air force and go overseas, and who at a later time did go overseas and joined the Royal Air Force. These were Canadians, and in some instances they were killed. Some of them had married English women overseas, and had children. What will be the status of those women and children, when coming to Canada? Will they receive pensions the equivalent of Canadian pensions, although their husbands were not in the Canadian service?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: That is, a man who went overseas, joined the R.A.F. and married an English girl, or an old country lady-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: That sounds better.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
They are all good-
English, Scotch, Irish or Welsh. -This man, as I say, after marrying was killed in action. If the wife and mother returns to Canada with her children, will she receive a Canadian pension?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: My colleague the Minister of Pensions and National Health says yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Will that also apply to Canadians who went over after the outbreak of war and joined the R.A.F.?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Yes, if they were domiciled here before they went over.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: How much worse off financially is the young man after he becomes a commissioned officer than he was before?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I have not the figures, but I know a great many find that after they become officers they are not anything like as well off as they were before.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Does the minister not think something ought to be done about that? Surely a boy ought not to be penalized financially because he accepts a commission in the forces of his country?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: He is not.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I understand it does not apply in commissioning from the rank of sergeant, but it does apply when commissioning from the rank of warrant officer first class -and second class?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: No; I am informed it is just when commissioned from warrant officer first class. The W.O.l receives reasonably good pay. Although he does not have the privileges of the officers' mess, he stands high in the community, as a rule. I may say that he runs the army.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: And he is entitled to be called "mister".

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Yes. Then, he gets what is equivalent to an officer's uniform, and does not have to pay for it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: And he does not want to take a commission, either.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: As a rule he does not want a commission.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I am informed that
not only is this condition revealed on paper, but the results are serious in connection, with certain small matters. For example, a commissioned officer is expected to incur certain incidental expenses which, in the aggregate, amount to a considerable sum of money, and constitute a deduction from the money he receives. So that, although on paper he may receive a certain, amount, he is actually much worse off financially. Is there any definite information on the point?

War Appropriation-Air Services

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: He usually has a somewhat higher standard of living. I suppose his messing is better than it would be if he were a non-commissioned officer. My experience, however, is that the N.C.Os. usually live just as well as the officers. However, the officer has to pay more for his messing privileges- although I do not think the messes are as expensive in this war, either in the air force or in the army. I can give my hon. friend the rates of pay for N.C.Os. and officers, if he wants that information. I must say to him, however, that I do not know just what extras the officers would be called upon to pay, apart from their generally higher standard of living.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: It is my opinion the minister should institute a rigid investigation into the matter, and see that there is a sufficient difference in pay to make it financially worth while a accept a commission.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I shall be glad to do so.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: There is a machinery for liaison with the Canadian personnel, including officers, N.C.Os. and other ranks, serving with the R.A.F. in the United Kingdom. I met some of the officers who were doing that work. Is there any similar machinery elsewhere in the world?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: With respect to messing, there was some discussion a year ago in connection with air force messes. That discussion, which appeared in the English press, stated1- whether true or not-that some of the English RA.F. messes were very expensive. I think the average messing in an army mess could not, by statute, go above three shillings a day. That was the maximum- messing we were charged in the army. But I understand that in the air force some messes ran as high as fifteen shillings a day.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: In war time?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Yes, in war time. At
least, that was the complaint in the English press. It was brought up in the House of Commons at Westminster at the time. Has the minister any information on that?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
No, but I shall be glad to
look into it. Fifteen shillings a day is a lot of money.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
There is an order saying that two shillings a day is the maximum. So far as the hon. member for Lethbridge is concerned, no R.C.A.F. man- suffers by having a commission. The highest pay for aircrew warrant, officer is $5.75 a day, and the lowest pay

for aircrew pilot officer is $6.25 a day. This is how the R.C.A.F. differs from the R.A.F., because in the R.A.F. the man does lose pay by taking a commission.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Could the minister give information respecting the liaison machinery?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Yes, we have liaison officers. We have a headquarters at Cairo, one at Naples, one in India, one in Tunis, and liaison officers in about a dozen different parts of the United Kingdom, if I am not mistaken. The hon. member for Vancouver North could tell us about that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
There are a couple in
London.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Yes, about half a dozen.
There are about a dozen different liaison or district officers who are in touch with Canadians in R.A.F. squadrons.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: And if they find a Canadian who is, shall we say, unhappy, because of being in an R.A.F. squadron, they may make recommendation to have him moved to another squadron?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: That is what they are appointed for.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: With respect to the allowances granted officers, N.CO's and airmen in Canada who do not live on the stations, it is my understanding that any officer when stationed in Canada is allowed to live out, provided his wife and family live near the station. In such event subsistence allowance is granted to him. Is the same privilege granted N.C.O's and airmen? That is, if an N.C.O. is fortunate enough to be stationed at No. 5, which is near the city of Brantford, is he allowed to live out? And if he lives out, is he granted subsistence allowance? Is there any limit to the number of N.C.O's who can live out? If so, is there a limit to the number of officers who may live out?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I am informed that, with regard to both N.C.O's and officers, the answer is broadly this: If there is room and accommodation in the station, while they may live out if they choose, they do not receive subsistence allowance. They can live out with the permission of the commanding officer, but they do not get any subsistence allowance. That allowance is given to them only when there does not happen to be room on the station, when there is no accommodation for them and they are obliged to live out. I understand that this is the common practice throughout all the services.
MARCH 6, 1944	[T* T	1199
War Appropriation-Air Services

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Is there any immigration restriction on the wives of R.A.F. Canadian nationals coming to this country? Has the minister any knowledge of just what is the immigration policy in that connection?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: How do you mean?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I am referring to a Canadian national serving overseas with the R.A.F. Can his wife enter Canada?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: That would come under the Department of Mines and Resources.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: She would have to get an exit permit from the British government.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: He would be a Canadian who had been domiciled in Canada, and I would think by marrying him she would become a Canadian. However, the question of citizenship is somewhat involved. I have heard it discussed in the house many times, but I could not really give my hon. friend an answer offhand.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: There are a couple of questions I should like to ask in connection with this item. First, what is the basis of the inequality in flying pay as between officers and non-commissioned officers? As I understand it, where an officer and a noncommissioned officer are travelling on the same plane, the first receives $2 flying pay and the second receives only seventy-five cents. What reason is there for this difference? It has become the subject of considerable complaint.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: It is a fair question but I have not the answer. I shall see what I can do about getting it for my hon. friend.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
It is something
which cannot be justified. The officer receives considerably more pay than the non-commissioned officer and yet the two men are in the same plane. Up until last year there was considerable complaint over the fact that non-flying officers were able to secure exemption from income tax by flying a certain number of hours. I understand that a new rule has been put into effect whereby nonflying officers, administrative officers and the like, can be designated by their commanding officer as officers to whom exemption is to be granted, even though they are not flying.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
My hon. friend is perfectly right. We cannot now be made the object of accusation that we are now flying in our income tax, so to speak. There has been created a certain number of what are known as annotated positions. These positions call
for a considerable degree of flying. They have not been established by the grace or pull of the commanding officer; they have been set up by the air member for organization working with a committee of officers of the R.C.A.F. They have decided that certain positions shall be annotated and the occupants thereof exempted from income tax during the time they occupy such positions.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Is it not a fact that there are quite a number of officers occupying these annotated positions who do little or no flying? By flying I mean to accompany pilots on flights. By being appointed to these annotated positions they have been able to secure exemption from income tax which otherwise they would not be able to get.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I shall have to get a report on that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: The minister possibly can give us an answer that will cover the situation by telling us the number of administrative officers who fill annotated positions and who thereby secure exemption from income tax although they are not actually engaged in flying.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I am told that they must be general list officers and not administrative officers.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: That is the point I am making. The information I have is that certain administrative officers have been annotated and that as a result they are exempted from income tax. I should like to have the number who have received exemption by being placed in these annotated positions, the number who have received exemptions even though they have had less than fifteen hours in the air accompanying crews in one year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I should like to pursue a little further the question asked by the hon. member for Cape Breton South with reference to widows of Canadians who went overseas and married women there. The hon. member inquired as to their eligibility to enter Canada. The Minister of Mines and Resources is in his place and perhaps he could give us an answer. I see he is now listening. I realize he has nothing to do with this department, but may I tell him that a few moments ago the hon. member for Cape Breton South asked the minister a question in connection with the admission of old country women who had married Canadians who were in the R.A.F. and who had since become deceased. The hon. member wanted to know if such women would be admitted to this country without
War Appropriation-Air Services

difficulty, and I understord him to say that there was some difficulty about their entry. The minister could not give a full' answer because he did not know. Perhaps the Minister of Mines and Resources could give us the answer.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Unless the minister wants to answer I do not believe it would be in order. He has not his officials before him and I really think that question should be allowed to stand.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Can he not enter the debate?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Certainly, but this has nothing to do with the item before the committee.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: The minister appears to be anxious.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I repeat that it has nothing to do with item 2. If the minister wants to answer it is up to him.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: One department at a time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: The minister can take part in the debate if he wishes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I want to make my point clear that this question has nothing to do with the item under discussion.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I have a case in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: If I understand the question aright, I see no reason why the lady could not be admitted to Canada, assuming that she comes within the requirements of the Immigration Act. There are prohibitions in the act against entry of certain people, but if the lady is not in any prohibited class I see no reason why in due time she should not come to Canada.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: There could be nothing controversial over the minister's statement.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: If a lady overseas marries a Canadian, she at once becomes a Canadian, so far as our immigration laws are concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: No; that would not overcome the prohibitions in the Immigration Act. Take, for instance, a person afflicted with epilepsy. That person would be prohibited entry under the act. But assuming that the lady in question can meet the requirements of the act, I see no reason whatever why in due time she should not be permitted to come to Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I wish to thank the minister for interjecting and answering a question that already had been asked by another hon. member.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I should like to 6ay a few words with respect to the matters raised by the hon. member for Lake Centre. He may have given a wrong impression as far as certain non-flying officers are concerned. There are non-flying officers, gunnei-y instructors, navigation instructors, signalling instructors, for instance, whose duties entail travelling around, and they are deserving of all the flying pay they get. I must join with the hon. member, however, in his suggestion that no administrative officer should secure exemption from income tax because he travels from one place to another in an aircraft. Let me give an example that happened to me quite recently. I had an opportunity to go for a flip in a Canso-I had never before ridden in a Canso. Seventeen other officers piled in and we had an enjoyable flip. The next day the adjutant asked me for my name and number so that he could post me S2 for a flip for which most of us would have gladly paid S5. The time has come, I think, to cancel special flying pay for non-flying personnel.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Would my hon. friend pardon me. We are now talking about exemption from income tax.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I am talking about flying pay. It is double-edged. Not only do they get exemption from income tax but S2 extra as well.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Flying pay is a different thing. That applies to all the service.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I think the minister has mistaken my point. Administrative officers who take casual flips ought not to get S2 extra a day for that, and exemption from income tax as well. It is a very nice bonus for them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Do they not have to be on the general list?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
No. Any non-flying officer who can claim that he is flying on duty-and it may be a very flimsy reason-gets $2 for that flip and the N.C.O.. and an airman seventy-five cents, and some of them run up quite a respectable sum in a month. Flying in an aeroplane is as safe to-day as travelling in a bus or train, except for those who are flying over Europe or are on operational duty. I would suggest that flying pay for non-flying personnel, other than navigation men, signal
I Mr. MacNicoJ.l

War Appropriation-Air Services
men, bombing and gunnery men, should be eliminated, and for all flips. The time has come to end that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Both at home and abroad?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: The pay regulations to which my hon. friend refers have been in existence for a long time, since pre-war. That is to say, under the regulations any officer or airman who goes on a duty flight gets $2 a day for flying. If my hon. friend were detailed for duty in Montreal he would get $2 for his trip there. But-if there has been abuse of the regulations such as my hon. friend mentions, of a man taking a trip in a plane just to get flying pay, I am glad that my hon. friend has called my attention to the matter. I can assure him that it will not happen again, and the boys will have to pay for their flights. But I do not see how I could overcome, without serious difficulty, a pay regulation which has been in effect for quite a long time and which provides that even though a man be on the general list, and his position is not annotated, if he is detailed for duty somewhere else, he gets $2 for flying to that particular place, if he is an officer, and somewhat less if he is an N.C.O. or an airman. But that is not the point my hon. friend brought up. His point was that in some way they evade payment of income tax.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: If they do it often enough, they evade payment of income tax and get the $2 for the flip as well.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: The $2 a day is a different matter. That is the practice and has been in the regulations for quite a long time, and I could not promise to change it without perhaps having to turn the whole service upside down. But I will certainly look into the abuse of annotated positions referred to by the hon. member for Lake Centre.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: And will the minister give the committee a list of the annotated positions?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I think a number of members have received letters from various air observer schools on behalf of civilian pilot instructors. They have taken some pains to make a case with respect to income tax, comparing their duties with similar duties in the ferry command. I do not rise to do more than simply ask the minister for the explanation which must underly the position which the government takes with respect to income tax. I would be very glad if he will enlighten the committee on that.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: There has been a concerted drive put on, and I think I have answered every member who has written me a letter about it. The reply is one of those formal ones. I will bring it down for my hon. friend to-night. If it is not satisfactory I think the only thing for hon. members who are being asked by these civilian instructors to present their case would be for them to present it to the Minister of Finance. I have made my reply and I shall be only too glad to read it into Hansard to-night.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I think the minister ought to do that, and if there is anything further to be done when the estimates of the Minister of Finance are before the house, we can deal with the matter then.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Are there any regulations on the subject of messing with respect to R.C.AT. personnel in Canada? From time to time I have received complaints from different stations that at some stations the food is not so good and there is a fixed messing fee, while at other stations there is no messing fee. Where there is a fixed fee, a monthly deduction is made from the pay cheque.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: This applies to other than officers?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Just to the rank and file below warrant officer. Is there any regulation that permits those administering an operational station or training school to make a deduction for messing from the pay cheque of any of the personnel below the rank of officer?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I gave instructions about a month ago to abolish that. It had been hanging fire for six months.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: It was abolished a month ago?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Yes. It is six months since my hon. friend called my attention to it and I determined that the practice should be abolished. There were, however, certain reasons for it which I felt were not very strong, and eventually I got my way.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: There is no regulation to-day which permits it?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: There is a regulation prohibiting them from doing it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
With regard to the point raised by the leader of the opposition, probably all of us have received these letters from civilian pilots. I should like to point out one thing that is not mentioned in the letter. A sergeant pilot who goes on leave as a civilian pilot to an air observer school gets $300 a month. A sergeant pilot who stays with the an' force and flies over Europe gets $105 a



War Appropriation-Air Services
month. I think most hon. members will agree that civilian pilots can afford to pay income tax.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I will not give any answer, now, if that is satisfactory.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I was not raising any question, but merely asking for information. So many hon. members have received these letters from time to time that I thought it was a matter about which the committee ought to know something. I am much obliged to the hon. member for Vancouver North. I think most of us who were not fully acquainted with the circumstances in this connection would like to have the facts put on Hansard for our information.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Before we pass this item
of pay and allowances there is a matter about which I intended to speak to the minister privately and personally. I believe it has already been brought to his attention, but he might be able to give us some further information. It has to do with young men who join the air force and are sent to places like Ottawa, and other centres, to the technical schools and colleges for training. These boys are put on subsistence, and frankly I think the rate is very low. It does not come near to paying their expenses. Here in Ottawa the allowance is $1.25 a day, and these boys are paying $1 for their room, and the other twenty-five cents is all they have, if it is not supplemented from some other source, for their meals. Possibly the minister is making other arrangements.
Mr, POWER: I am afraid I cannot make any other arrangements, except to see to it that as few as possible of our men are on subsistence allowance, and I think, as time goes on, there will not be many. It is almost an impossibility to work out a system of subsistence allowances in different zones or in various parts of the country. What a man gets is $37.50 a month: it is not enough for the time he stays here, but these men do not stay very long in congested centres.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Well, they stay for two or three months. I think some arrangement should be made if possible to put them in barracks.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: We are trying to do that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I do not think they should be wandering around at night.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
But I could not raise the
subsistence allowance.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: It is better to have them in barracks. They are under discipline and receive better care and attention.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Has the minister any
control over the way in which food is served in the R.A.F. camps? As he knows, some of the air force are transferred to R.A.F. camps, and the complaint has come to me at different times-I have a boy in the service -that the food service in these camps is not comparable with the service in R.C.A.F. camps.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Does the hon. member mean overseas, or in Canada?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I mean in Canada. I imagine that the food supplied to all the camps is the same. Presumably the objection is to the way in which it is put up and served, but there seems to be a great difference in the way it gets to the men, as between R.A.F. and R.C.A.F. camps.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I have heard that complaint frequently. The food is the same.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
In order to obtain information may I ask the minister a question?
I have not had an opportunity of interviewing any of these men. I simply passed on the letters that I received in order to get the information in a public way. How do the air observer schools or the other training schools recruit these civilian instructors? From what group in the air force are they taken?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: They are largely sergeant pilots who have gone through the air training plan; are given leave without pay, and are then employed at civilian schools.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In most instances are they men who have had operational service overseas?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Not any of these.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am quite sure that most members of the committee are a little confused when the question is answered in this way. Are these sergeant pilots who find themselves in the position of civilian instructors picked out or chosen from the sergeant-pilot class because they have special adaptability or special training? How do these men happen to get leave without pay and then be taken on, as the hon. member for Vancouver North says, at S300 a month? What is the test by which these men are chosen?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Originally when we started the civilian schools these men were civilian bush pilots or men who had done some flying before the war. For some reason or another they did not care to come into the R.C.A.F., or perhaps they did not qualify for aircrew on some ground or another; therefore they were employed by these schools. As time went on, they either did not join the R.C.A.F., or disappeared from the scene and got other jobs in other civilian occupations, so that we had to fill those schools either with these men whom we took into the R.C.A.F., blanketed them in as civilian instructors, or with some of our own graduates who, for some reason or another, were perhaps not fit for overseas or who had probably joined through the civilian schools and had been sworn into the R.C.A.F. with that purpose in mind. I am not sure about that. I know that at one time the civilian schools could not get any more civilian pilot instructors. They came to us and we said: "We will take them all over and make
iMr. Power.]
them R.C.A.F. men." In that way we probably absorbed some who otherwise would not have joined the R.C.A.F. at all. We did that in order that we could have some control over them. We can send them overseas.

speechtext: They are available for operational work overseas?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence

When the committee rose I was on the point of asking a question in connection with travel. At Christmas time I met a number of young airmen in my riding who had just returned from British Columbia. Two of them told me-and maybe others went through the same experience-that they were well into Alberta and some in Saskatchewan before they were able to get a berth. In other words, they had to sit up all the way from Vancouver, or wherever they boarded the train in British Columbia, to well across

War Appropriation-Air Services
the prairies. I suppose the same condition applies to those who board trains at Halifax or Saint John or anywhere in the east. I have been wondering if in the case of holidays like Christmas and Easter or stated holidays when large numbers of these young men are returning to their homes in the east and west, the government could1 not provide sleeping cars, especially for airmen or service personnel returning to their homes in the central provinces from both east and west coasts.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not think any of the services have ever provided berths and meals for personnel travelling on leave.

But where there are such numbers travelling at Christmas time from British Columbia or Halifax does the minister not think something should be done? These men are coming to their homes in.Ontario and other provinces, and they are entitled to accommodation. As I said a moment ago, it would only be fair to provide one, two or three cars, or whatever is required, wholly for the service personnel. I speak now of the air force, but the same thing will apply to the others as well.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I think that would be a matter for the railways. There is always a shortage of accommodation at that particular period of the year. It would be for the railways to arrange that, provided the men would pay for their berth and meals. The services do not pay.
The minister is so persuasive with the railways and everybody else that I have the notion if he would interest himself in the matter something would be done.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Very often I would like to get a berth for myself, but I cannot get away with that.

I am speaking of special
occasions, not ordinary trips such as the minister and I take. When a large number of these young men are returning after a holiday, such as Christmas, two or three cars could be provided for them if an effort were made.
Mr. HARRIS Danforth):	As the minister
probably knows, it is a practice in the United States, something that has grown up as a courtesy rather than under any rules or regulations, for civilians to stand aside until such time as men in uniform have found accommodation on the trains. I should like to take this opportunity to say to ithe people of Canada through you, Mr. Chairman, while this matter is being discussed1, that it would not hurt the civilians of this country to step aside, when men in uniform are boarding trains, and let those boys have everything that is coming to them. I agree with the minister that it is a matter for the railways. I do not suggest that the railways should make any rules or regulations in this regard, but I do ask the civilians of Canada, who are not doing nearly so much in behalf of Canada as those lads are doing, to step aside on station platforms in order that those in uniform may go through first and have their choice of accommodation. Then we can take what is left.

I should like to add a word in a different connection. Only to-day I received a letter from which I should like to read a few lines:
I wonder if some day you would ask the hon. Minister of National Defence for Air why air force personnel are not allowed any travelling time with their fourteen days annual leave? The navy and the army get it, the latter get seven days paid travelling time. This has always struck me as rather unfair and I can see no good reason for our being denied this privilege since the same taxpayers and government are paying us all. Last fall when the new K.R. (Air) was issued travelling time (8 days) was included as one of the new regulations, but shortly after this was, so I am told, cancelled.	-
Then this girl goes on to give an instance of a girl going from Toronto to the west coast, stating that she had only five days at home out of the fourteen days leave. Are members of the air force treated differently from members of the army and navy; and, if so, why?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
When these appropriations were first before the committee I raised the matter which has been mentioned by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, and I should like to support what the hon. gentleman has said. This particularly concerns those who travel from, the part of the country from which the hon. member comes. Travel takes so much of the time that there is not much time left for these boys and girls to spend at home, though they have planned and saved1 for months in order to make the trip; and every-

one knows that it is not very' easy to save money on the pay they get in the armed services. I do not think there can be any very good reason for longer withholding from' those in the air force the privileges which are granted to those in the other branches of the armed forces. I understand the situation to be as outlined by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, and perhaps the minister would be good enough to explain it.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I do not think it is quite as has been stated. I must say that I am surprised to find the situation to be as it turns out to be, because I was always under the impression that the other services complained that the air force had too much leave. This is the information I am given. A table has been prepared setting out in detail the regulations of the army, navy and air force with respect to the leave. That table is attached to this statement, and I can place it on Hansard. It is pointed out that the information contained in the table, with respect to the army and navy, has been taken from the latest available regulations and orders of the navy and army, and it is suggested that before this is tabled and used it might be advisable to have it approved by the appropriate army and navy representatives. I think this has been done. As indicated in the table, no travelling time is granted by the R.C.A.F., except in the case of special leave at isolated units. Similarly, no travelling time is given by the army, except in connection with embarkation leave or furlough, when personnel of the army warned for overseas service may be granted leave or furlough sufficient to provide two clear days at home. All personnel of the R.C.A.F., when posted overseas, are granted fourteen days embarkation leave irrespective of where their homes are located, and this period is considered sufficient to allow personnel proceeding on this leave, even from one coast of Canada to another and return, to have the same, if not more, time at home than is given to army personnel on embarkation leave. I
I am not prepared to discuss that, because it may be a pretty broad statement. However, my information goes on to say that it is therefore considered that in general the army and air force regulations with respect to travelling time in addition to leave are on the same level. The navy does grant travelling time in addition to normal leave. This is considered justified in view of the fact that the larger proportion of the personnel of the navy are serving at sea and leave must be taken from whatever port the ship may arrive
tMr. Graydon.]
at and at a time when leave can be granted. The conditions of service of Royal Canadian naval personnel who are serving at sea differ from personnel of the army and air force serving at fixed units in Canada, and because of this, travelling time in addition to normal leave is justified. It is also considered that reasons to justify the granting of travelling time in addition to normal leave to naval personnel are not present to justify the granting of such travelling time to army and air force personnel.
Then there is a long story here setting forth the different kinds of leave: annual leave, embarkation leave, disembarkation leave, even political leave, with the conditions in the three services set out. If the committee would like to have this table on Hansard I would have no objection.

1.	Annual Leave.-Personnel who are continuously employed on flying duties are eligible for 14 days leave with pay once every six months. Personnel not employed on flying duties are eligible for 14 days leave with pay once every fiscal year. Leave not taken may be accumulated in exceptional circumstances, but this is not encouraged.
2.	Granting of.-Normally leave is not granted during the first six months service of officers and airmen, and trainees other than aircrew are not given leave until completion of training. Leave may be granted to aircrew trainees when time is available between courses and in such cases is not charged against annual leave.
3.	Isolated Units.-On completion of a tour of duty of not less than six months at isolated units, personnel are eligible for seven days special leave in addition to annual leave authorized, together with travelling time actually required for the return journey to the mainland or railhead, but not to exceed five days in any case.
4.	In the case of personnel posted to isolated units on the east coast, arrangements are made for them to take annual leave prior to posting, and they are not granted annual leave during their tour of duty at such isolated units. This does not apply to aircrew. While such postings are for an indefinite period, in practice personnel are posted away after a tour of duty of from 12 to 18 months. At the request of the A.O.C., W.A.C., this restriction w'as not extended to the west coast.
5.	Indefinite Leave.-Indefinite leave without pay is no longer granted, and applications for this type of leave to return to essential industry are treated as application for discharge, provided a certificate is obtained from national selective service that the individual's services are

essential to the efficient conduct of the industry concerned, and that there are no other personnel available with comparable qualifications.
6.	Farm Leave.-A.O.s.C. have authority on the C.O.'s recommendation to grant spring farm and harvest leave to personnel who can be spared from their duties, up to a maximum of two months, for each type of leave. Such leave is without pay and allowances, including dependent's allowances.
7.	Sick Leave.-Sick leave is granted by
C.O.'s on the recommendation of a medical board.
8.	Compassionate Leave.-Compassionate leave may be granted either with or without pay, depending on the circumstances of the case.
9.	Embarkation Leave.-R.C.A.F. personnel and C.T.E. trainees from Newfoundland are given 14 days embarkation leave, including travelling time, irrespective of the leave destination. Where possible personnel other than trainees proceeding overseas on posting, or for a period of not less than six months on temporary duty, are given 14 days embarkation leave.
10.	Repatriation Leave.-Personnel who have carried out a term of two years on ground duties overseas or aircrew who have completed an operational tour, and who have been returned to Canada for other than disciplinary or medical reasons, are given 30 days leave including travelling time. Personnel rvho have carried out a term of duty extending for a period of at least six months overseas but less than two years in the case of groundcrew and aircrew who have not completed an operational tour, and who have been returned to Canada for other than disciplinary or medical reasons, are given 14 days leave, including travelling time. In exceptional cases such personnel may be given leave not to exceed 30 days.
11.	Passes.-Periods of absence from duty of 48-hours or less are considered as a pass and are not charged against leave entitlement. Some flexibility is necessary under active service conditions, and the exact number of off duty pass privileges is left to the discretion of C.O.s. including decisions as to whether these pass privileges are to be given on week-ends or during the week.
12.	Transportation on Leave.-Personnel proceeding on authorized leave may be granted one special reduced fare annually to return to their bona fide homes, at a cost to themselves of one-third of the existing reduced rate which is
round trip at the price of a single fare. In addition, a similar warrant may be issued on embarkation or disembarkation leave.
13.	Furlough warrants, i.e., return ticket for the price of a single fare, may be purchased by personnel in uniform or in possession of Canadian passenger association form 95, which is issued by the adjutant of the station, and these tickets are available without retsriction as to number.

speechtext: I do not know how the time would figure out, but the army get two clear days at home, as I understand it, while the air force get fourteen days all told.

speechtext: I am not arguing for the army. They get two clear days at home while we get fourteen days to make the trip, stay at home and return.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister is making a better case than I thought he would make, but even at that it falls short of being a convincing case. I do not think there should be any discrimination because a person happens to live far away. After all, one Canadian is just as good as another in the air force, and I do not think a person's leave should be cut down by virtue of the distance he may have to travel. speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am rather inclined to agree with my hon. friend. I had an idea that they got more leave than this, and I do not believe this is very satisfactory.

I have always wondered how the posting of recruits in the air force was arranged. For instance, we may find someone from Toronto posted to Vancouver, and someone from Vancouver posted somewhere else. There is probably a very good reason for this, and that reason may have much to do with the difficulty of arranging leave. I had thought that in connection with the first part of the training-I think they call it pre-I.T.S., do they not?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes.

I have often wondered why the boys should be sent so far away. Probably they like to go, because they enjoy seeing the country-and when I say that I speak from experience. On the other hand, they are a long way from their homes. Is there any other reason why they are posted at long distances from home?

While I may not be in order, I should like to ask a further question. Last year the minister gave us an idea of the length of time it took to train aircrew of one kind or another; that is, pilots, gunners, navigators, radio operators and so on. I do not -know whether he would care to give us that information again, and if he does not I shall not press for it. I believe, however, that the information would be of interest, because he has told us the courses have lengthened materially from what they were last year.
Then we must consider the cost of transportation for the forces. They do get a reasonable rate when they are travelling on leave, but I do not think it would cost the country very much to give them free transportation either on annual or on embarkation leave. I do not believe that privilege would be abused. Probably in respect of a 48-hour leave it is proper to have them pay on a reasonable basis; but when they have either embarkation or annual leave I can see no reason in the world why they should not have their transportation free, and receive decent accommodation.
The hon. member for Danforth has just spoken about civilians giving up their places in cars to air force .men, and men in the army and naval forces. I agree with the hon. member, and I believe some other arrangement ought to be made whereby these lads might be given better consideration. I have seen them standing all the way from here to Toronto on the afternoon train. It does not seem right that they should have to do that.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence

I would say that postings present a very difficult problem. We have been Hying as far as possible not to post men too far away, and to keep them within the command at which they entered the service. But it often happens that a course has to be filled. A class may be opening on a certain date, and has to be filled by pupils who have entered their training in Ontario. The course in question may, for instance, be in Alberta, and we have to send men out there. The same applies all along the line. Sometimes it looks easy on paper to say that so many hundred will graduate at a certain date from such-and-such a school from, let us say, Toronto. They may have gone to E.F.T.S. at some point close to Toronto. In that event it would be St. Catharines. Or, in respect to Ottawa, it would be Pendelton. After going through that school they would move to S.F.T.S. at Uplands. But it does not always work out that way.

Our people are constantly striving to prevent extra travelling by posting the men, in so far as possible, within the area whence they started their training.
With respect to the length of time required, I can give only approximate figures, because the time is constantly changing. At the time this estimates book was prepared, namely around October, a pilot in service flying training school stayed sixteen weeks; a navigator-B stayed in navigation training school twenty weeks; a navigator-W stayed in navigation training school twenty-two weeks; a straight navigator stayed twenty weeks; air bomber, six weeks; air gunner, twelve weeks-I believe that has been raised. Then, W.O.A.G., six weeks, and flight engineers two weeks. On top of that I believe there are twenty-eight weeks somewhere else.
There have been constant changes, and in order to estimate how long a man would be in training I would have to find out in what category he was, the availability of places in schools, and_ the backlog in reserve. Sometimes they stay two months on tarmac duty before they enter their training schools. Then they go from that school to elementary, on to service flying; from there to operational training, and so on. I would not guarantee that anyone would become a pilot nowadays under eighteen months.
