I have been trying to find out for three years where Mossbank camp is getting its water supply.

To return to the question of pay, the boys I met last summer enlisted as aircrew and were receiving $1.30 a day, with no extra pay as tradesmen. They were working for a contractor * at $1.30 a day and were getting nothing extra. I was wondering if the contractor was paying anything to the government.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: They should not have been working for that if they were aircrew; I cannot understand aircrew being on maintenance work. Perhaps my hon. friend would give me the details.

The men were
groundcrew, working for the contractor and receiving regular air force pay of $1.30 a day.. They were just new recruits.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The money coming from the contractor goes to the receiver general. These men must have been doing the same kind of work they would have been doing as ground-

War Appropriation-Air Services
crew at the station. Had they been doing tradesmen's work they would have received tradesmen's rates of pay.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
5. Personnel, supplies and services:	Food,
medical and dental stores, clothing and personal equipment, $38,515,252.

Is there any regulation specifically covering recreation facilities at air force stations? I know of one station where moving pictures are brought in and operated by an outside concern, and the boys at that station are obliged to pay an admission fee of twenty-five cents to see the show. My recollection is that when the last canteen fund committee sat, it was understood that all canteen funds were to be used to provide recreation facilities in and around any of these camps and stations, and I am wondering if the boys at the station I have in mind are not being exploited. Upon making inquiries I find that at some stations the boys are charged nothing, and at others they are charged ten cents, but the station I have in mind charges twenty-five cents. It is not because the entertainment is extraordinary; it is just the regular run-of-the-mine show as provided at all the stations and camps across Canada. Would the minister care to comment on that?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I would think it was a civilian moving-picture organization using one of our recreation halls and getting it rent free, light free, and accommodation free, and that if any profits were made they would go to the canteen fund to be used for the benefit of the men. I have never heard of twenty-five cents being charged, but it might have been done without my knowing it. ' It is a matter of arrangement between the canteen committee and the person showing the pictures.
It is the station at Sydney I have in mind, and the boys there think they are being exploited.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I shall certainly be glad to look into the matter. My impression is that any profits would accrue to the canteen fund. I cannot see how we would give the use of the hall free, and free light and heat, if necessary, just for the purpose of making some money for a civilian concern. If that is being done, it will certainly be stopped.

Does the minister's department get a report on these canteen funds? I understand that the reverse is true; the canteen funds were to be used for that purpose instead of the canteen fund being provided in that way with extra profits. Is a report on canteen funds at the R.C.A.F. stations made to the department?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes; every quarter our financial people receive a report on canteen funds from every station, from every unit.

In 1942 a special committee was appointed to consider the whole question of canteen funds. At that time the committee was advised that one per cent of the gross sales of all canteens operated by the R.C.A.F. was paid to the R.C.A.F. benevolent fund. It was further represented to the committee that the only persons entitled to benefit from the R.C.A.F. benevolent fund were members of the permanent force. The committee recommended that no further payments should be made to the benevolent fund until provision was made that all members of the Royal Canadian Air [DOT] Force now serving should be allowed to participate in that fund. I would ask the minister if that recommendation has been put into effect.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I would say yes: the benevolent fund now is for the benefit of all members of the R.C.A.F., past, present and future.

I have had complaints from boys who have had their "medical" in the different air force pools and have then been told that they would have to report at a certain time. When they report they are lined up, perhaps with ten or more other boys, to go through, and then one, two or three of them are called out and told, "Well, now, you have not a full medical", or some other reason is given, and they are not allowed into the air force. Perhaps these boys have been counting for three or four months on going in, and it is certainly a great disappointment to them. Could the minister arrange that these boys shall have a full medical?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Have what? A full medical?

Yes.
I do not know the reason for this practice.
It may be that there is something about a boy which determines them not to accept him, but it works a hardship on these lads. Many of them have had going-away parties attended by a number of their friends, and it is pretty hard for them to return to their ordinary life again.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: If my hon. friend will tell me where this has occurred I shall be only too glad to check up with the medical officers.

I shall do that. I put a question on the order paper some days ago with regard to the clothing supplied to our boys overseas. It appears that

War Appropriation-Air Services
Great Britain supplies these uniforms. Some of the boys complain that the uniforms which they are getting there are not of as good quality as those supplied here. Is there a chance of their receiving uniforms from Canada? They state that the clothes they get overseas are a little coarser and are not as comfortable.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: We have had that complaint before. We have made representations to Great Britain. My hon. friend will realize that if we started distributing uniforms and all the other equipment overseas we would have to set up a pretty big establishment, a kind of ordnance corps, overseas, and I do not think that at this stage we are justified in doing so.

I
hardly meant that. There are friends of these boys who are quite willing to buy clothes and send them over. Would they be allowed to do that?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I have never heard of any "other ranks" in either the army or the navy or the air force buying their own clothing, and I am sure that if we permitted such a thing there would be a howl of indignation from this house which I would never get over.
There are some who would be willing to supply the clothing.
Do the Royal Canadian Air Force make their own messing arrangements or are they supplied by the army service corps?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The army service corps feeds us.

There are only one or two of these training schools about which I have had complaints, but one about which I have heard several, is Lachine. I do not know whether the minister has had any complaints along these lines. I was wondering whether the R.C.A.F. have general supervision, over and above the army service corps.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: We cook the food and serve it and all that. We get our supplies from the army service corps, and we look after all the messing.
You look after all the cooking?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Certainly, and wash the dishes.
Has the minister had any complaints about that sort of thing at Lachine?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Not lately. Off and on, I suppose, I have had complaints with respect to pretty nearly every station of the air force. As soon as we get a complaint we hand it on to the chief messing officer of the particular command, and he makes an investigation and reports to me. Usually the matter is cleared up. I have not had anything lately with regard to Lachine; that is, not for the last six months or a year. It may develop rapidly, and sometimes it evaporates just as rapidly when checked up.

These lads who have been to camps all over the country usually have nothing but praise for the food; they do not think it could be bettered. But there are just one or two exceptions, among them Lachine. That is why I asked the minister if there is something wrong with the place, because I have had several complaints about it.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Lachine has changed its organization. It was a manning depot; it is now a "Y" depot, and probably the whole organization of messing has been changed in the last two months. If my hon. friend receives another complaint and will let me know, we shall have a look at it.

I have a question with respect to Canadian personnel serving in the Royal Air Force overseas. I understood the minister to say that the British government supplies them with their personal equipment, rations, et cetera. * What is the financial arrangement with respect to that? Does the Canadian government reimburse the British government? Also, what is the position with regard to expenditures, say, on ammunition, wastage in aeroplanes and equipment which our men who are attached to the R.A.F. are using?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is all in the lump sum payment of $345,664,944, item 13, maintenance of overseas squadrons for the year 194445. It also includes all our personnel overseas.
What is the arrangement with regard to the personnel in the R.A.F.? Is that paid on a per capita basis?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes.

On page 394 of Hansard I find that item 5 in the list of estimates contains "personal equipment", as well as "personnel". The words "personal equipment" are not in the typewritten list. If the item as

War Appropriation-Air Services
detailed on page 394 of Hansard is correct, what is included in personal equipment?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: My hon. friend is talking about item 5 at page 394 of Hansard?
Yes.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It reads: "Personnel supplies and services: food, medical and dental stores, clothing and personal equipment." In my sheet the words are "personal supplies." I think it is the same. The list is: "Personal supplies and services, clothing, rations, barracks stores, laundry and medical."

Personal equipment is'
left out?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence

Are
there any psychiatrists in the medical service of the air force?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence

many of those are overseas?

British Hansard that twenty-three per cent of the men discharged from the British army were discharged for psychiatric reasons. I wondered if the minister had a good staff from over there?

I should like to ask the minister a question with respect to medical services Tendered to aircrew injured in Canada. Is there any discrimination as between ranks? It was brought to my attention recently that in an accident a sergeant pilot and a wing commander were injured. The sergeant pilot was placed in the public ward in one of our hospitals, while the wing commander, who was not injured as seriously as the sergeant pilot, was given a private room with a special nurse. I am wondering if that discrimination exists.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am inquiring about the answer. I do not know. It may well be that that happens. I shall look into it. Is the hon. member speaking of an accident that happened recently at St. Hubert?
Yes.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I shall find out.

The question I am about to ask may not arise out of this item, but it arises in connection with the minister's state-

War Appropriation-Air Services
ment with regard to the number of Americans discharged from the Canadian air force. How many United States pilots are there in the Canadian air force at the present time?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I can find out. I think between two thousand and three thousand were returned home. Some are represented as deserters. Some of them have done very well in their own service, but they did not say, "Thank you, good-by," before they left, and they were put down as deserters. I am clearing them up.
In the casualty lists that we receive there are a great many Americans.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I can get that figure, but we shall have to subtract from that number the number who have returned to the United States forces. I did have some pretty clear information as to what the number was a couple of years ago, but it has slipped my memory since that time. They were very numerous. I shall put it on the record.
Are musical instruments supplied to the bands? It is very important that we have lots of bands.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: We have lots of bands. I am told by my Scottish and musical friend, the Minister of Pensions and National Health, that we have the best bands in Canada. He ought to know.
I do not agree with the minister; I know of many pipe bands that are a little ahead of that one, though it is a very good band.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I should say my colleague
was not a good judge of music; he plays the bagpipes.

Some people understand music and others do not; you have to be Scotch to really understand it. I just wanted to know whether these instruments were supplied, because I think it is wondferful to have bands of one kind and another.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
We have bands both here
and overseas.
Do you supply the instruments?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes:

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.

Are all these instruments and materials purchased through munitions and supply?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes; everything.
Does the minister indicate his preference as to whether these instruments should be purchased in this country or in another country?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I am told that this signal
and wireless equipment is always purchased in Canada if we can get it here, or in other countries if we have to go there.

The minister does not
indicate any preference?

He gives Munitions and
Supply a free hand to supply that which the R.C.A.F. require, according to their specifications?

speechtext:
Yes; but I would imagine
that in things such as signal1 equipment our technical officers might say that such a gadget was better than another gadget. I really do not know.
That was what I wanted to know.

I think for a long time it
was not a question of indicating where this sort of equipment could be obtained; it was a question of trying to get people to make it. I think that was the great difficulty, and in the earlier stages we were very much bothered with that.

A considerable change
took place in the course of last year, I think.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I would not know; we
simply send our financial encumbrances and our requirements to Munitions and Supply, and they make the purchases.

I think I shall have to crave your indulgence, Air. Chairman, in asking this question; probably I should have asked it under item 2. It has come to my attention that wireless mechanics require anywhere from twelve to fifteen months to finish their course and that they are kept on the basic pay of $1.30 a day until the course is completed, whereas in most other branches of the services the pay is stepped up from $1.30 to $1.40 and then to $1.50 at the end of three or six months. Has the minister given any consideration to stepping up the basic pay of the wireless mechanics at certain periods of their training, on the condition that their progress is satisfactory?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I am told that all our men
automatically get up to $1.50 after six months service.

Is a wireless mechanic brought up to $1.50 at the end of six months?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes, so I am told.

My information is
that they get their first increase when they complete their course.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not think that is right, but I shall check into it. My officers tell me that they get their increase after six months, but I shall make sure that this is accurate.

This afternoon the
minister intimated that he would make a statement in connection with prisoners of war.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I shall do so when we get a little farther along. I am waiting for it to come from upstairs.

In item 6, at page 394 of Hansard, the words "line construction, etc." appear, but in the typewritten sheet those words are left out. Is line construction included in the word "communications" on the typewritten sheet?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The same thing is meant, but perhaps they did not consider line construction so important this year, because it is not proposed to build as much as we built last year. We had a very big programme of line construction last year and it is not quite so big this year; we are only completing what has been started. Any change in the phraseology was not done with intent; it is supposed to mean the same thing. This item would cover the construction of lines which we have to carry out this year.
But there is a considerable increase in the item.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
That is largely a carryover on account of articles and equipment ordered previously, sometimes as long as two - years ago. There was a very great shortage of manufacturing capacity in connection with signal and wireless equipment. When it started to come in we got a lot of it, and I may be quite frank in telling the committee that we received some that is not of much use to us, since it is almost obsolescent by the time it comes in. This has almost become a problem with us, because developments in reference to wireless are going ahead so rapidly that the production of one particular gadget is just about completed when a better one comes on the market and we almost have to throw away what we thought was the latest thing up to that moment. However,
the increase is largely due to what is coming in now, with the increased productive capacity both here and in the United States.
Have more teletype machines been installed this year?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is included in this item, but we only show rentals of teletype machines, no new purchases.

speechtext:

7.	Ammunition and bombs, $18,175,000.
Why would there be a reduction in this item when we are just about to enter the most vicious phase of the war?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: This is for Canada only. The bombs and so on that we use on the other side are obtained from the R.A.F. We have a goodly supply of bombs for practice and for our western hemisphere operations in connection with anti-submarine patrols and so on.
Under what item shall we find the estimated amount to be paid for material purchased from the R.A.F.?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence

War Appropriation-Air Services
And gliders?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am told we have to provide machines in connection with the training at Shilo, but I do not think we are doing much of it at this time. It has nothing to do with the machines overseas.
This is just for Canada?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes; this is for Canada. Offhand I cannot say how much we are providing for machines to carry parachutists. That is all we do, in fact; we carry the parachutists to their targets, and drop them.

asked the Minister of National Defence and he did not give me an answer. Now the minister does not give me a satisfactory answer.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence

I cannot for the life of me recollect whether or not we may have two, three, four or five aircraft at Shilo, where parachutists were trained at one time. If we have, I shall let my hon. friend know. But that would be the limit of our responsibility in training the paratroopers.
These other boys go to the United States to train, do they?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: They are army; they have nothing to do with us.
That is all American?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes, it is all American.

Mr. Chairman, I notice that this item provides for an expenditure of more than 3188,000,000 for aircraft engines and spares. We ought to have an explanation of this item. What kind of engines are these? I know they are aircraft engines, but of what particular kind? This is a huge amount of money, and there ought to be some explanation for a sum of that size.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
My hon. friend will see that there is a reduction of about 372,000,000 from 1943. The reduction is accounted for by reduced aircraft requirements, owing to a revision of our defence of Canada plan, because a more favourable situation, and to the end that we shall require no further provisioning of aircraft for the British commonwealth air training plan. We shall have enough aircraft. We have provisioned for, I think, up to 194S or 1946, so that we shall not require to purchase more. Moreover, aircraft contracts have been liquidated more rapidly than anticipated during 1943-44. That is to say, we are getting

in more aircraft than we anticipated, in the fiscal year 1943-44, thereby reducing the amount of long-term liability to be liquidated in 1944-45. But we still have a tremendous amount of aircraft to pay for in 1944-45. Aircraft for training and aircraft for combat units on the coast are included. I do not wish to give numbers, but I think we have reached the stage now in the war where we can to some extent give numbers of aircraft.
The aircraft position for this year shows that the total number to be delivered is 960 aircraft. We now have over 11,000. I shall not give the exact figure, but we have over that number. That is 60 single-engine aircraft, and we have over 5,000. That is only in the air training plan. Of twin-engines we expect delivery of 862, and we have nearly 6,000. That is in the air training plan alone, and does not include the defence of the coasts.

And that is not for
overseas?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No, not for overseas at all.
What is the wastage of them?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I cannot really say-and I do not know whether I should say. In other words, we expect the total of over 900 planes to be delivered this year, and in 1945-46. We have nearly 12,000 already, in the air training plan alone, exclusive of what we need for western hemisphere defence operations, and for overseas. Those figures I do not care to give.
This is a summary for air training alone?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes, air training alone.

What types of aircraft are we using now for air training? Up and down the years the minister has told us about the different kinds of aircraft. We have heard a different story every year. What types does this amount cover?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I would say that we are now using Cornells, chiefly, for elementary training. Then, for single-engine trainers we have Har-vards and Yales. For twin-engine training we use Ansons, Cranes, Oxfords, Beechcraft and Lockheeds. For bombing and gunnery trainers we use Battles, Bolingbrokes, and Lysanders. For wireless trainers we use Forts, Harvards, Yales, Norseman. For single engined transportation we use the Norseman aircraft. For operational trainers we use Hurricanes, Cansos, Liberators, Mitchells, Mosquitoes, Beechcraft, Dakotas, Venturas, Baltimores and Swordfish.

War Appropriation-Air Services
How many of these are made in Canada?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Cornells and Ansons-and Lysanders were. Bolingbrokes, too, were made here; and Harvard, Norseman, Hurricanes, Cansos and Mosquitos. I believe that is about all.
Is any part of this item of more than $188,000,000 connected with the Department of Munitions and Supply? How much of it is supplied by that department?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: We buy everything from the Department of Munitions and Supply-every cent of it.
Does any of this amount appear in the estimate of the Department of Munitions and Supply, later on?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I do not think so, no.
Included in this item is an expenditure for aircraft engines and spares. Have we yet undertaken the manufacture in Canada of aircraft engines?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The answer is no.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: To follow up the question by the hon. member, has any move been , made by the government with respect to setting up a plant and the necessary equipment for the purpose of manufacturing aircraft ' engines in Canada?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I should much prefer that that question be asked of the Department of Munitions and Supply. All I do is use the engines I can get, wherever I can get them and when I can get them. If my hon. friend would ask the Minister of Munitions and Supply, whose job it is to procure these things,
I am sure he would get a much better answer than I can give him.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I am not so sure about that. I only ask the question of the minister because in all our aircraft industry in Canada, and all our development in connection with aircraft manufacturing, the one great bottleneck which will occur, perhaps, in the post-war period is that we shall have to go elsewhere to get the engines. The minister will recall that in a former debate-I am not sure but that it was 1942-the question of replacements and overhaul was stressed as being a very serious problem for the air force. I remember at the time listening with no small degree of gloom to the minister's statement as he uttered it. It seemed to me, a layman, that our position with respect to repairs for the machines we had became a serious matter. Would the minister tell us now whether we
are able to get ample planes, and able at the same time to repair and overhaul them, so that there will be no difficulty as far as our men in training are concerned, and no interruption of that training?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: At one time back in 1941 there was a really acute situation. I expressed the fear in this house, and I had reason to do so, that the opening of some of our schools might have to be delayed and that others might have to curtail their operations owing to lack of spares, No. 1; lack of repair facilities, No. 2, and lack of new planes coming in, No. 3, which probably should be No. 1. We had a critical period for several months, but since then we repaired a lot more of the aircraft in our own establishments. We recruited men, turned out mechanics and put them into our own establishments to do the work. Fortunately we were able to get spares although, as I say, there was a shortage for some considerable time. Aircraft had come in at a greatly accelerated rate. There is no difficulty in securing training aircraft at the present time, except that operational training aircraft, which are of the same type as those used in combat overseas, are hard to come by.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: How many hours of flying does a training plane complete before it has a general overhaul?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: There is airframe and engine overhaul. It runs from 800 to 1,200 hours.
That would vary with the machine?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes.
I think two years ago the figure given was 400 hours.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That has been raised since.
A few moments ago the minister gave the number of training planes. Would that number include those used in the R.A.F. schools?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The figure of 11,000 or 12,000 would include the planes used in all R.A.F. schools.

How many overhaul
stations are there in Canada, and what portion of this $188,000,000 is for overhauling?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I cannot say offhand how
many establishments there are for overhauling, but the amount is $41,500,000.
Is most of this work done in government- or privately-owned plants?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
This $41,000,000 would be
civilian contractors.

War Appropriation-Air Services
How many contractors are doing this work for the department?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I get a report every week as to the progress of civilian contractors on overhauls, but I do not happen to have it here. I could put the list of civilian contractors on Hansard. They are arranged for by the Department of Munitions and Supply; I have nothing to do with them except to pay them.

What portion of this
expenditure would be for engine spares? We would then have the break-down of the three items.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The $41,000,000 is for repairs, The estimated cost of additional aircraft is $19,000,000. The estimated1 cost of additional engines is $6,000,000. The estimated cost of spares for new aircraft and maintaining existing equipment is $17,000,000. That gives a total of $43,000,000. Some equipment, such as guns et cetera, would go in, totalling $830,000. Then there is $32,000,000 for airframe overhaul; $10,000,000 for engine overhaul, giving a total of $43,000,000. From this we deduct the work done in our own repair depots to the extent of $6,000,000 which would give a total of $37,000,000 under the plan, alone. Under western hemisphere operations, the amount for overhaul of airframes is $4,000,000, and for engines, $1,000,000. From that total of $5,000,000 we knock off fourteen per cent for repairs we complete in our own repair depots. That gives a net figure for repairs to engines and airframes for western hemisphere operations of $4,300,000. The cost of aircraft to be purchased during the fiscal year for the British commonwealth air training plan will amount to $11,224,000, and engine spares to be purchased will amount to $934,600.

That is not a very
satisfactory break-down. Surely the minister can give us the totals for aircraft and, for engine spares in addition to the total he has given us for overhaul of some $41,000,000.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I gave it for aircraft as well. My officers will work it out. The trouble is that it is divided between the western hemisphere operations and the plan.

This item totals $188,-
000,000 and so far we have had but two figures, one of $37,000,000 and another one, $41,000,000. We are not finding any fault, but I think we should have a proper break-down of this $188,000,000.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
As regards the $37,000,000
and the $43,000,000 it was just my mistake in reading the figures. The total cost of airframe overhaul and engine overhaul was $43,000,000,

but we as a service do $6,000,000 worth of work. This is charged to another item as pay and allowances because our own men do the work, so that the total under this item would be $37,000,000.

The minister understands that I am not finding any fault with him because he is really a good minister, but his officials should be able to give him the exact break-down of this figure. That is what they are there for.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: We have lots of figures.
When the minister asks for an expenditure of $188,000,000, his officials should be able to hand him a slip showing the break-down.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
We have it broken down, but in a different way. We have enough mathematicians to give all the break-down possible. I may be able to satisfy my hon. friend in this way.
For the joint air training plan it is estimated that it will cost $67,163,710 for aircraft in 1944-45; for home war, that is western hemisphere operations, $79,292,650; overseas, $1,100,550. That is aircraft for our own use overseas; it has nothing to do with combat aircraft. Then, under the air training plan, overhauls for 1944-45 will cost $37,054,145; overhauls for western hemisphere operations, $4,336,490. Overhauls for overseas are in the total figure. That makes a total of $188,947,545.

There you get the
$188,000,000 odd.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I was going to break it down still further. For the joint air training plan the total, in round figures, for aircraft and engines is $67,000,000; for overhauls, $37,000,000, making a total of $104,217,000. Then, for western hemisphere operations, aircraft and engines, $79,292,000, and overhauls, $4,000,000, making $83,000,000 in round figures. Then for overseas, for transport aircraft, $1,100,000. That makes a grand total of $188,947,545, which is the figure I started out with. If my hon. friend wants any more break-downs I shall have to see what I can do for him.

The minister has my
sympathy. We have been voting millions so easily and generously from this side of the house that perhaps everybody is getting a little befuddled with the magnitude of the figures.
I wish to ask a question with reference to overhauls. The government has some crown plants making aeroplanes, one at Mal-ton and one out on Dufferin street, Toronto. Those are two very large crown plants.

War Appropriation-Air Services

speakerposition: Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: DeHavilland is not a crown plant.

Has any of the overhauling and repair work been done in crown plants? I understood the minister for air to say a few moments ago that all the overhauling was done by private companies. Why not use some of these huge crown plants for overhauls and repairs?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: DeHavilland is turning out a certain type of fighter aircraft and Malton is turning out bombers.

speakerposition: Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Repair work interferes with production. It is much more economical to do overhaul work in separate plants. To put overhaul work into production plants interferes with the production line and is very expensive.
I helped operate a big plant for a long time and we did not send our overhauling out to be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Perhaps you were not very busy.
We had 925 men on our payroll.

speakerposition: Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: We have 8,000 at Malton.

And we paid them out of profits from production in a private plant. We did not have a government to get the money from. It is a different proposition. We had to run it as a business. The minister has been in business, and when he looks back to his own system of operating business he knows very well that he had to pay for his repairs and overhauls out of profits. He would have gone to the wall if he had not done so.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In regard to overhauls and repairs there was a time, not recently perhaps, when Yales and Harvards were overhauled at what is now Victory Aircraft, but that was perhaps when production was being changed over from one type to another.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
11.	Miscellaneous stores and equipment, including machine guns and other armament, $15,992,000.
The minister said that some of the air fields would be discarded. Is that right?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Yes, but not under this item,
of course.
This item deals with maintenance, stores and equipment, which would be removed when the air fields were discarded.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes; that would be under care and maintenance. I suppose my hon. friend refers to barracks stores and things of that kind.
Yes.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I would hope that my hon. friend the Minister of Pensions and National Health, when he is starting new hospitals or other institutions, would take advantage of the fact that we have spare beds and bed equipment of all kinds which would be suitable in these other institutions.
I have suggested before that he take over some of the staff houses for hospitals.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I hope he will.

Because after the war they will not be used, and some of them could be taken over right now for hospitals. There might be a chance that under this item the minister might have some old planes and engines. We have some wonderful air cadet corps throughout Canada, and those boys would be tickled to death if they had an aeroplane engine.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: They have got them.
Not all the corps.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Let my hon. friend ask for one and I shall be glad to give him an aeroplane and an engine any time.
Good! That is fine!

Almost all the items of equipment that I can think of are covered by items 5, 10 and 14, and yet here is an item of over $15,000,000 for miscellaneous stores and equipment. Can the minister tell us just what the items are?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I have a list here: Small arms; A/C machine-gun mountings; ground machine-gun mountings; ordnance and ordnance sights; guns and spares; machine-gun firing gear; machine-gun sights; filling and positioning machine; special tools for armament equipment; armament ground instructional equipment; bomb gear; range finders; Browning guns; miscellaneous electrical stores; cable and wire electrical; aircraft electrical stores-
That is enough.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I have two pages more.

It is armament, in other words.

War Appropriation-Air Services
Mr. LOCKHART r Will the chassis of aeroplanes be available to vocational and technical schools as the minister said they would be for cadet corps?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: While I am in a generous mood, because the committee has been very good, and am willing to give away a lot I do not think I would have authority to give away to civilian institutions crown property that belongs to the R.C.A.F., but if my hon. friend will make application for what is required for a vocational training school I shall do the best I can to get it to him somehow. The air cadets, of course, are in a different position. They belong to the air force and it is easy to give them anything.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Not at the present time.

It will be handled
through some crown company, I suppose.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It will be turned over. Perhaps my hon. friend would like me to explain the set-up of surplus asset disposal?

I shall be glad to have a brief review of the matter. But I would again impress on the minister that there are lots of useful avenues into which such articles as these chassis could be turned instead of being broken up into scrapiron. They would be extreme!}' useful in such places as vocational schools if some arrangement could be made with the provinces.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
That is why I said that it is easy enough for the R.C.A.F. to arrange for the disposal of some of its own stores to one of its own components, namely the air cadet league, but it is not so easy to dispose of them to civilian organizations. We have a new set-up under order in council, namely an assets disposal committee, operating under the Minister of Munitions and Supply, which decides on all policies with regard to surplus

assets. If I have spare aeroplanes, barracks stores, engines, rubbers, shoes, clothing or what-not, they are handed over to the surplus assets committee, which decides on the policy generally to be followed out in disposing of such assets. If it is decided that they shall be disposed of by sale they are handed over to the crown assets corporation, which actually does the selling.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: War Assets Corporation.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: War assets. But the committee first deals with the policy. My hon. friend, for instance, would know that certain vocational schools require a certain type of equipment to assist in their training. He vtfould probably ask the air force if he had reason to believe that we have surplus supplies of this kind, and we would pass the request on to the surplus assets committee, which could then say, "Well, in the general interest of the country any of these surplus assets could very well be given to such an organization rather than be held for sale by the crown corporation."

speakerposition: Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: May I just correct that? Crown assets cannot be given away. That has been decided.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister for air has beaten you to it. He has given a couple of aeroplanes away already.

speakerposition: Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Air cadets' property, of course, is still retained in the crown. No one can give away crown property, not even the committee.

I wish to make my
position clear on this matter of giving equipment away. I am not asking for something for nothing, but I would point out that when the war clouds were gathering, before the year 1939, small groups of men banded themselves together and established civilian flying schools in connection with municipal airports, and certain types of aeroplanes, such as antiquated Moth planes, were used, although they were always falling to pieces. I recall that there was some difficulty about getting possession of one or two of these chassis, which proved1 a great inspiration to the young boys who at that time were going through the vocational schools. I cannot substantiate this, but I am reasonably certain that my information is correct, that on two occasions old Moth planes were sold for scrapiron in spite of efforts which were made to have them turned over to groups of boys who were working ip vocational schools and were very much interested in aeroplanes at that time. I suggest to the minister that he make sure that whatever crown organization is formed will not make any difficulties

War Appropriation-Air Services
about dealing with municipal bodies, and will not allow some of these planes of obsolete design to go into scrap when they might be an incentive to the training of the young boys who are coming along and who will do our commercial flying in the days to come. I point out that we did have difficulties a few years ago, just before the war, obstacles owing to what may be called red tape. At least let it be known that some of these obsolete types are available, so that application may be made.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
We are making it known
now that we shall have a lot of them.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
With respect to the
matter of disposal of assets such as the minister has described, this matter arose in a similar way when the appropriations relative to the army were before the committee. While I have not personally had any requests from persons in the air force for an opportunity of procuring machines when the war is over, I have one or two requests with respect to the disposal of jeeps to members of the armed forces.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I want one myself.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Well, the. minister would look pretty good in a jeep. It is a vehicle very appropriate to the minister. I believe that one of the things which men in the air force will want, to do when the war is over is, continue their flying. It would seem- only fair that if aeroplanes are to be disposed of, some of them should be available for the men who want them, provided, of course, they are suitable for use in civilian operations. Has the government any policy in this matter?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I have known quite a few
officers to say that they would like to buy a small Moth plane or something of the kind to go travelling around in after the war. I assure my hon. friend that there will be, as he can readily understand, surplus aircraft of all sorts and conditions, and that the corporation presided over by my colleague, the Minister of Munitions and Supply, will, I think, be glad to receive offers for air frames before they are broken up, because there would not be much salvage in breaking them. up.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Perhaps I should not delay the _ committee at this time on something which I fancy does fall in the category of the debate which would normally be expected to take place on the War Assets Corporation. Pefhaps I need not proceed any farther with that, but I should like to content myself with this one observation in connection with salvage. Let us not forget
as a parliament and as a government that at the moment the public is ready to spend money if it is spent for war purposes; but the pendulum will swing-

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It has swung already.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Yes, I think the minister is correct in that. The pendulum will swing more and more. The whole question of waste and the utilization of the assets that have been bought is becoming of great importance as far as the public is concerned.
I think the government might well take into consideration the position in which we shall find ourselves with respect to public opinion in that regard. After all, while the public is ready to put money into these things to-day for the purpose of winning the war as speedily as possible, the same public in years to come will be-as the minister says they are now- more alert and more conscious of the disposition that is to be made of those assets once the nation has no further use for them in connection with the war or before they become obsolete or something of that kind occurs. I am hopeful the government will make sure that such economies with respect to salvage-and there are 'a lot of economies possible with respect to salvage that the two ministers now in front of me will readily attest-will be carried out so that the public will not get the idea, as the years roll by, that this material is to be thrown on the market at bargain prices, that no attempt will be made to overhaul it and put it into salable shape; in other words, that the whole matter will 'be let go in a reckless form of abandonment.

A few moments ago the minister referred to the .company. Did I understand him to say that it had been set up? My information is that it has not been set up. The Minister of Munitions and Supply will know. About ten days ago I was in several plants and I saw some surplus equipment. In one of those plants I learned that a company was to be set up, and the gentleman who told, me said that perhaps in a few days it would be brought before parliament. I am heartily in accord with the setting up of a crown company to conserve the vast quantity of equipment which is likely to be a hundred per cent usable and can be resold. I do not suppose the company has been set up. I have heard the names of some of the men who are to be chosen to head that company and they were all first-class men. If the Minister of Munitions and Supply names these men to form the company. I shall be glad to support the

War Appropriation-Air Services
proposal. The minister spoke as if the company had already been set up.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The order in council is
passed.

I do not want to ask
the Minister of Munitions and Supply if it is so or not until he wishes to announce it. I was under the impression it would be announced in parliament.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The order in council is passed. I am not sure that the company has actually been incorporated, but the order in council dealing with all this was passed some time ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
Perhaps. I can explain this
a little further. The company has been functioning for about six weeks. It was set up by order in council as a matter of urgency. The surplus problem was becoming rather acute. Later in the session there will be legislation dealing with the whole matter.

That is the information I received. It was said that later on it would be announced in the house. It should have been announced in the house. Parliament has been in session now for four weeks or more.

What is the item? Mr. MacNICOL: The hon. member says, "the next item." I should like to tell him something. The opposition has supported the government in putting through large sums of money. We could not alter the amounts if we talked for a month, but the minister has been kind and courteous. We have been trying to be kind and courteous, and we have tried to help him put through his estimates. There is no use in saying, "next item."
I think the hon. member said he wanted to go on with potatoes.

Pardon me. I thought the hon. member said, "next item." I apologize to him now. Let me return to the crown company. The crown company has been set up by order in council but has not been announced in parliament until to-night; at least I have not heard it. I would appreciate it more if it had been brought to parliament earlier. Anyone who knows anything of business knows that such a company would have to be set up, but in courtesy to the House of Commons, it should have been announced here first. I should not have to be told of it in a plant.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence

Operation and maintenance expenses are paid to civilian operators on the basis of schedules which have been prepared, and take into account estimated normal expenditures for each type and size of school. In the event that the actual expenditure for a given period is less than the target expenditure, eighty per cent _ of the saving reverts to the Royal Canadian Air Force and twenty per cent is retained by the company. The amount retained by the company cannot be distributed but must be held in reserve account until the termination of the contract. Arrangements have been completed recently with the air ministry of the United Kingdom whereby six additional Royal Canadian Air Force Squadrons will be established overseas by the transfer of certain complete squadrons at present organized in Canada for operation within the home war establishment. We shall have to buy planes for those six, too.
The present and future strength of the Royal Canadian Air Force overseas squadrons in accordance with present operational plans

would be, roughly, forty-four squadrons, divided into heavy bomber squadrons, fighter squadrons and coastal command squadrons. Heavy bomber squadrons, of course, cost more money, because the bombers are very expensive.
Provision has been made in the 1944-45 estimates for the above-mentioned squadrons, together with ancillary units as follows:
Capital charges, six squadrons_ $ 13,667,285

Maintenance charges are billed to Canada quarterly by. the United Kingdom air ministry on the basis of annual squadron charges which are dependent upon the type of aircraft and the operational role in which aircraft are employed by the Royal Canadian Air Force squadrons. The basis of squadron charges and the elements of cost included therein have been carefully reviewed in the United Kingdom by responsible Royal Canadian Air Force officers, and are considered to be fair and reasonable in accordance with past experience and available information. The amount included for air cadets is $1,012,480. The question whether or not we could allow these air cadets to fly in their two weeks' training is one which, I am frank to say, is giving me a great deal of concern. Sometimes I feel like saying yes, and more often I feel like saying no. Frankly, last year I was inclined to agree, and to obtain a waiver from the parents. Shortly before that, however, we had several severe accidents in training-not the cadets, of course; I am referring to our own airmen. I received a flood of letters from parents of boys who were in training, blaming us for the equipment, or the maintenance, or carelessness of people. The result was that I changed my mind with respect to the cadets. I thought that if we were to be blamed for the accidental deaths of men actually in training, whose job it is to take those risks, we might be blamed far more by parents of boys of fifteen or sixteen years. Even though the parents might sign a waiver, they might complain. That is the state of mind I am in this year.
Last year, over and above all this, there was the very good reason that we would not have had the time. This year, with more schools- although some of them will not be schools until later on-and with more instructors available, it would have been possible. But there is a risk involved. A great many parents might sign a waiver, but if the boy of certain parents were unfortunately killed or badly injured as a result of an aeroplane accident, the parents would never forgive either the minister or the air force for having given their boy a chance. I am open to conviction [DOT]either way on the subject.
I agree with the minister that this is a very important decision to make. However, it is a live question. There is no decrease anticipated in the cadet programme ?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I can answer that. That was one reason why the company was formed. Normally, as the minister says, each department disposed of its own, through a salvage officer, who is an officer under control of the treasury. We had a certain -number of surplus aeroplanes, and we had to hand them over to the salvage officer. He called for tenders, and the only tenders he could get were for this small amount. It was after we went through this experience-although we had been thinking of it for some time- that it was borne in upon my mind just what the situation was. One of my officers said that the disposal of surplus assets would become one of the greatest rackets since the invention of loaded dice, unless someone took charge of it pretty soon.
It was, after the last war.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence

It is not my baby, it belongs to the surplus assets corporation. I became interested at some stage of the matter because we found that to dispose of assets of this kind by simply calling for tenders would get us into all kinds of trouble and lose much money for the country.

speechtext: That does not come under this.

Last year the agricultural food board designated where milk should go, whether to cheese factories or to conden-series. I have had a good many complaints recently from farmers who have had to send their milk to cheese factories. Last fall, when usually a number of factories would be closed, a subsidy was placed on milk for cheese factories, and consequently a number were kept open during the winter months. The complaint that I have from a good many farmers' in my constituency is that the price of milk going to the cheese factories is not comparable with the price of milk going to condenseries. There is a good, deal of dissatisfaction over that and a number of farmers appealed to me just over the week-end, saying that they had applied to the agricultural food board to be allowed to change over from sending their milk to the cheese factory but were refused permission to ship it to the condenseries. I have in my office a table which was prepared over the week-end, showing the difference in the amount the farmer receives according to whether his milk is shipped to a cheese factory or to a condensery. I have not it here because I did not know this item was coming up to-night. If I remember the figures correctly, a man who had twelve or fifteen cows last year showed me by a table that he had lost almost S200 by having to ship his milk to a cheese factory when he could have shipped it to a condensery if the food board had given him permission. On top of that, over the last

several months the condensery plant at Napanee has been shipping a good deal of milk to the city of Toronto for distribution, and all the milk shipped from there to the city of Toronto pays a premium to the farmer of twenty-five cents a hundred. So that the farmers, if they had been allowed to ship the milk to Toronto for distribution, would have benefited to that much greater extent. I appeal to the minister to give this matter consideration, because it is of much concern to the farmers. I should be glad to let the minister have the table I have in my office or present it to the committee at a later stage.

I understand that the different uses to which the by-products of milk might be applied could be investigated under this item. For instance, the use of whey. Whey comes from the production of cheese. In some instances it is worth quite a considerable amount for feed; but if it gets too sour, if it is not properly cared for after the cheese is made, it is not nearly so valuable. Then there are the other by-products of the manufacture of butter, such as skim' milk powder and casein, and the different manufacturing outlets which I suppose should be investigated to see how much the price of them does add to. the value of the milk. In the mines and resources estimates, under "national research council," a rather large sum of money, something over $300,000, is being appropriated, as the minister indicated at the beginning of his estimates, for research on agricultural matters. This dairy research, together with bacteriological and dairy research, as proposed1 under the increased vote indicated in the mines and resources estimates, will then be carried on under the auspices of the national research council. Does it not raise the whole question whether the council is the organization under which money voted for agricultural research should be expended? The minister will find himself, I believe, with research being done in the national research council under a vote in the mines and resources estimates, and he will also be saddled with another research branch having to do with problems of bacteriology and dairying. This matter was brought up before and received some attention in the discussion. I am inclined to think that those who took part favoured the retention in the Department of Agriculture of the research facilities which were being thus'expanded. If the minister would give an explanation in this connection it would be helpful.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
It will not affect at all the matter of research as it is spoken of here. This has always been carried on in the Department of Agriculture under its usual activities, and will so continue. But there was a vote of $200,000 put in the agriculture estimates last year, in a supplementary vote, which was set apart for the purpose of doing certain research, more particularly in connection with oil-producing plants and the growing of different products particularly in the west and the extreme east. That vote does not appear in the estimates as they now are. It is my intention again to submit a $200,000 item to the treasury board and to the government in connection with our supplementaries this year in the hope that it will be continued. I am not now in a position to state whether it will
be continued or not. But there is an item, as has been suggested, of something over $325,000 in the Department of Trade and Commerce to carry on certain research. It is not this type of research: it is to try to find new uses, namely commercial uses, for different farm products, such as the utilization of wheat in the making of rubber. It may be that not much money will be spent on that particular object, but it will be things of that type- using wheat or grains for some other purpose -and a vote of that kind does not interfere with this one.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister is satisfied that it should be left with the national research council?	'

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I am satisfied that some of it has to be. That which is associated closely with industry is probably better left with the national research council. Where .the question is whether one can produce some particular type of plant in a certain area of Canada, I think it should be investigated by the Department of Agriculture, and the same may be said of projects such as the crossbreeding of plants to determine whether one can get better varieties for growing in this country.

A new type of experimentation has been going on in the preservation of meat and the sterilization of milk and so on by electronics. Is that being undertaken by the National research council? Probably the question would come under the item affecting the research council, not the Department of Agriculture.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: On all that kind of research we work in cooperation with the national research council. We ask them to do work for us and they do it. That was the intention in setting up the council, that all the research work which could be done by the ' research council would be done for all departments of government, and our department, in common with all others, gets as much done as we possibly can.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, let us be clear. The item which was carried before was item 7, but the minister was good enough to allow me to ask a supplementary question. That item is carried, but not item 8. Item 7 having been carried, let us call it eleven o'clock.
